speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES-CANADA-AGREEMENT RESPECTING DEFENCE FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table an exchange of notes between the United States of America and Canada constituting an agreement on the subject of war surpluses and related matters. In relation thereto I should like to make the following statement.
Both the United States government and our own have found it advantageous to simplify the procedure followed hitherto in disposing of defence facilities and equipment provided in Canada by the United States. They have therefore agreed that Canada shall pay the United States $12,000,000 (U.S.) in return for which there is transferred to the Canadian government a long list of defence facilities and equipment, the original cost of which was approximately $59,000,000 (U.S.).
These installations and materials include items related to the Alaska highway and the northwest staging route, to weather stations in northeastern Canada, movable property reported to War Assets Corporation under an earlier agreement, but not sold, and certain naval and air equipment which had been provided by the United States to the United Kingdom under lend-lease and which, when returned to United States account, remained in Canada. The price paid is a reasonable one, in view of the usefulness of many of these installations and materials to the armed forces and other agencies of government, and the agreement is regarded by both governments as a satisfactory settlement of a property disposal problem which otherwise might have been long drawn out and complicated.
There is an additional aspect of the exchange of notes which is important.
In order to provide equipment necessary for the training programmes of the Canadian armed forces, the United States government will endeavour to make available, surplus military type equipment up to a maximum value of $7,000,000 (U.S.). The agreement calls for negotiation between the two governments as to quantities and prices and will enable the Canadian armed forces to obtain much of the training equipment that they will require at figures considerably less than would be the case if orders had to be placed with manufacturers for new equipment.

subtopic: REGIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD FOR QUEBEC
REGIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD FOR QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	Was Paul Emile Marqiiette of Montreal recommended for appointment to the Regional War Labour Board by the Canadian Congress of Labour?

2.	Has the Canadian Congress of Labour requested the removal of Mr. Marquette from this position? If so, what action has been taken?

subtopic: REGIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD FOR QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	Yes. In February last the Canadian congress of labour requested that Mr. Marquette be removed from the Quebec regional war labour board.
On March 5, 1946, an official communication was received by the department from the Canadian congress of labour nominating Mr. T. Prezeau to replace Mr. Marquette.
On March 8 a unanimous resolution, which had been passed by the Quebec regional war labour board on February 26, was received from the board to the effect: "that Mr. Marquette should be maintained in office as a member of the regional war labour board, first, because of the lengthy experience he has had in dealing with matters pertaining to the control of wages-besides that which he has acquired since he is with the board-also because of the fairness and impartiality he has always displayed in the judgment of the applications which up to now have been presented to the board".
On March 12 the department notified the Quebec regional board that the Canadian congress of labour urged that Mr. Marquette be replaced.
The Quebec board was organized by agreement between the government of the province of Quebec and the dominion government. The necessity, therefore, for consultation between the parties in this matter will be appreciated.
On April 2 the names of Messrs. T. Prezeau, J. E. Corbeil and J. M. Bedard were submitted to the department by the congress for consideration.
On the same date, April 2, these three names were telegraphed to Honourable Antonio Barrette, Minister of Labour for Quebec, requesting that he indicate his choice.
On April 3 the regional war labour board for Quebec wrote the department repeating its recommendation of February 26 that Mr. Marquette be retained on the board for the reason that "his integrity and experience have proved to be most valuable to the regional board".
On April 3 Honourable Mr. Barrette wrote the department suggesting the appointment of Mr. J. M. Bedard to the Quebec regional war labour board.
On April 8 the dominion Minister of Labour had a telephone conversation with the Quebec Minister of Labour and the latter made it

Questions as Orders for Returns
clear that he wished to have Mr. J. M. Bedard appointed a member of the Quebec regional war labour board in place of Mr. Marquette.
Steps are therefore being taken to revoke the order in council appointing Mr. Marquette a member of the board and to recommend to the cabinet council that Mr. Bedard be named as his successor.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO QUESTIONS AFFECTING SASKATCHEWAN RIVER WATERSHED
PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO QUESTIONS AFFECTING SASKATCHEWAN RIVER WATERSHED
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of introducing legislation during this session to set up a permanent interprovincial board or commission on which the three prairie provinces and the dominion would have equal representation under the chairmanship of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or some other qualified person, to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible

Water Conservation
and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the matters referred to in the resolution are of such tremendous importance to the three western provinces as well as to all of Canada, that I hope out of this debate much good will result to the country generally. The whole economy of the western provinces is threatened by the presence of areas which may be described as arid or semi-arid, or, better still perhaps, as desert and semi-desert; and unless immediate steps are taken to reclaim these areas the consequences to the western provinces will be disastrous. I hope those who take part in the debate may bring home to the people of the three prairie provinces a keen conception of the situation as it exists to-day; and I hope proper emphasis will be given to the lowering of the water plane of the three western provinces. which is one of the main causes of these arid areas. I trust that the business men and financial interests of eastern Canada will take an active part in trying to reclaim these areas, because as a former eastern business man I am convinced that unless these desert and semi-desert areas of the west are reclaimed, the eastern companies will have great difficulty-in maintaining their present position, let alone bringing about any expansion.
I should like to give just two examples et what is resulting from our failure to reclaim these areas. I believe the census is taken in the western provinces about every fir? years, whereas the census for all Canada i? taken every ten years. Between the taking of the census of 1935 and the time war broke out in 1939, the population of the great central province of Saskatchewan dropped by some forty thousand persons. In my opinion that was a major disaster to Canada. Then in January last, on my way west, in a report issued either by the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Trade and Commerce, I saw an announcement that in 1945, notwithstanding the fact that the farmers received substantial prices for what they had to sell, the returns to the farmers of the . three prairie provinces were $186,000,000 less than those of 1944. That is another problem of major proportions, because if additional crops to the value of $186,000,000 had been produced the difference would have mors than paid for the programme I have in view in this connection. I hope every hon. member of the house will take note of those two striking figures; a loss of population of 40,000 souls in Saskatchewan alone from 1935 to 1939, and a loss through drought, principally
in Saskatchewan, of $186,000,000 in 1945 as compared with 1944. In my judgment these are staggering figures.
The only antidote for arid or semi-arid areas, or desert and semi-desert conditions, is water. Nothing else can reclaim such areas. A few days ago in an engineering article I read that deserts do not stand still, that they can be reclaimed by water but that if water is not applied, they march on. This article went on to say that what had been the great city of Timbuktu in north Africa is threatened with destruction by the continuing march of the Sahara desert toward the south west, and that already it has been partly destroyed. So our objective should be not only to reclaim but to try to arrest any expansion of these desert conditions.
Now may I say just a word about the resolution. It divides itself into four parts. I must confess that it could have been much better worded, but I suppose the ministry will have no difficulty in accepting the first division, namely that immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of introducing legislation during this session. As a matter of fact I am very happy to say that the estimates for this year contain the sum of $10,000,000 for this work, which is a substantial start toward reclamation. I believe that $10,000,000 can be divided up among several projects, and I shall deal with that later.
The second division has to do with the setting up of an interprovincial-federal board. Recently when I was in the west I discussed this whole problem with every engineer with whom I came in contact-city engineers, government engineers, and general engineers. At that time I had in mind that we might have in Canada something similar to the Tennessee Valley Authority in the United States, with which I am very well acquainted. What they have done is revolutionary in regard to expanding the economy of the seven states through which the Tennessee river flows. At the time I thought we would have to set up some such authority here. However, I must confess that I am quite pleased with what the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has done, and I have great confidence in the director of that organization, Hon. George Spence. However, the PF.R.A. legislation, which I believe was enacted in 1935, does not take in the whole of the area. It does not include northwestern Alberta or northeastern Manitoba, both of which would come under any project of the magnitude of that I have in view. However, I have no doubt the government can expand the control of P.F.RA, and if they should so decide, well and good.
Water Conservation

The next division of the resolution pertains to the participation of the provinces. The states do not participate in the T.V.A.-set-up; the United States government has financed the 'whole undertaking.

speechtext: I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if you can do anything to bring about a little better order. We cannot hear the hon. member at all down here; others are speaking almost as loudly as he is.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO QUESTIONS AFFECTING SASKATCHEWAN RIVER WATERSHED
speechtext:
I had in view the participation of the provinces in suggesting a separate board. I cannot conceive of works of this magnitude being carried on without the consent and perhaps assistance of the three western provinces, and I can see no reason why they should not participate and why their participation would not be helpful. Of course I am not going to tell the minister what he should do; he will use his own judgment in that regard. I merely point out in my resolution that to include the provinces in these works in my , judgment would be beneficial.
In my reference to the chairmanship of the proposed board I had in mind one whose decisions would inspire the utmost confidence throughout the country. I have suggested a judge of the supreme court, but I have noted a good deal of opposition to the appointment of judges to boards. If the government decided that the chief engineer in the department, the chief engineer under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, or the director thereof, in whom, as I said a minute ago, I have great confidence, would be suitable, I should have no quarrel with that decision. When I suggest the appointment of a judge I am not offering something which could not be altered.
The provinces are already acting. Each of the three western provinces has sent engineers -I am not sure whether they have sent their chief engineers, but information to this effect appeared in the press. Those engineers, meeting in Regina, have formed themselves into a small board. They cannot act, of course, because the Saskatchewan is a navigable river. I am sure however that their participation in the matter of western rehabilitation and conservation could not be other than helpful.
In the latter part of the resolution I refer to the conservation of water and the utilization of the eastern watershed in the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river. I shall proceed from that point, because it is with that matter I wish to deal particularly.
I have made as careful a survey as was within my power, both by foot and on horseback, of a considerable portion of the eastern

slope of the Rocky mountains. I learned- I was going to say with horror, because what I saw affected me in that way-about great acreages of fine timberland which had been burned. I learned that for years a minimum of 30,000 acres each year have been destroyed by fire. In consultation with engineers in the west I learned, and I have reason to believe what I was told, that the destruction of
30,000	acres a year in the foothills of the Rocky mountains, timber which had retarded the run-off of the- snows and water in the spring so that it was retained in a manner which permitted its flowing down the river more evenly, had a disastrous effect on the glaciers.
I have not sufficient technical knowledge about these matters to check on that information, but I was told by two outstanding engineers that the great forest fires on the slopes of the Rocky mountains, through the process of hurling soot on the glaciers, retarded the accumulation of those glaciers, with the result that they have shrunk to a considerable degree. I can see nothing but disaster to. the west if those glaciers shrink appreciably. Of course it would take a long time to bring this about-perhaps not in our time-but I do urge it is our duty, to the extent of our ability, to protect the generations which will follow us. One of the protections we could afford would be the preservation of the watershed of the Saskatchewan river, through the protection of the glaciers. A step in that direction would mean the restoration of vast areas of foothill forests which have been destroyed by fire, and every effort made to prevent future fires in the foothills of the Rocky mountains would be worth while.
As to the conservation of water, might I point out that I have been up and down all the important parts of the river, from its mouth to its source in the mountains. I travelled up as far as I could go, to view the Columbia glacier. In company with engineers I have seen many splendid sites for reservoirs. P.F.R.A. has issued some instructive maps and excellent reports which indicate that on the source rivers of the Saskatchewan there are about thirty-six splendid sites for reservoirs, some of which are large. I have in mind two which I inspected, one called the Whirlpool and the other the Gap. The Gap was located not far from Nordegg in Alberta, and the Whirlpool also in Alberta but much closer to the Banff-Jasper highway. Both these sites are large, each one capable of conserving about 380,000 acre feet of water. That is a lot of water, Your Honour. If one

Water Conservation
adds to those two the other thirty-four reservoir sites, he might well be convinced that we have ample opportunity in the source rivers of the Saskatchewan for this type of work. I have in mind rivers like the Castle, Old Man, Waterton, St. Mary's, High, Bow, Brazeau, Clearwater and Mistaya. One reaches all those rivers when making a survey.
So far as I can estimate all those reservoir sites on the head waters are sufficient to store approximately 10 million acre feet of water. That, too, is a lot of water.
In addition, along the main river there are many excellent sites. As hon. members are aware, the main river has two great branches, the North Saskatchewan and the South Saskatchewan. In consultation with engineers, and after inspecting as thoroughly as is possible by a layman-that is, outside of digging down below the water line-I can say that the site near the Riverhurst area, if it were developed by the construction of a dam 175 feet high, would back the river up 100 miles. And I am satisfied the average width of water at the top water level would be not less than three-quarters of a mile. One can figure by taking the top 50 feet of that reach that he would have available 2,500,000 acre feet of storage. I have seen other excellent sites, just as good as the one at Riverhurst. If one were to limit himself to only four such sites-and there are many more-he would have another ten million acre feet of storage-In other words, from what I have seen of the river and its source branches, there are reservoir sites capable of conserving twenty million acre feet of water.
When I think of the priceless necessity for water in western Canada, and think that almost every drop runs to the sea without giving any advantage to those great provinces -with the exception, of course, of what is dione in southwestern Alberta-I feel that we are confronted with nothing short of a tragedy. I am not blaming anyone for this. I know the country has a big load to carry, and that it cannot go ahead faster than it can secure the money for purposes of development. But let me point out.-and I shall develop this later on-that these projects are self-liquidating and in reality cost the country nothing.
For instance, let us consider what has been done in recent years in India. One often thinks of India as a backward country. 'It is far from that. Within the last few years in the province of Sind a very great irrigation work has been created. Water is stored behind the Sarda dam, and the main canals running frcpn that point are 4,177 miles in length.
Just try to imagine any canal in this country to equal that. Then let us ask ourselves how we compare with India. We will remember that in our childhood we read, times without number, about the tremendous loss of life in the Punjab, and the province of Sind, because of drought. In the province of Sind, behind the Lloyd dam, they have backed up sufficient water to irrigate five and a half million acres. In the Punjab they have their great irrigation works which irrigate millions of acres Of land. They have worked on the basis, and rightfully so, that these are self-liquidating projects which will pay for themselves and which will save millions of lives in that country. When I think of what I have observed in the west and what the people in the western provinces have come through, my heart Weeds. I am going to stay with this business as long as I am in public life. I am going to advocate the completion of these projects which will restore that western countiy.
When the house rose in December I was planning several trips. One was to Arizona to make a further study of the great Roosevelt dam and the Salt river irrigation works associated with it. Any one who has been in Arizona will have observed the vast transformation that has taken place in that formerly cactus-ridden state because of these irrigation works. The magnificent city of Phoenix has grown up where formerly nothing but cactus grew. It is a beautiful city of about
150,000.	people. Just fancy the returns to the United States from the production in that area, from sales tax and income tax from a city like Phoenix. It is a self-liquidating project which will not cost the country anything.
I was considering going to the west, although I was a little afraid of the winter-but I should not have been afraid, because I learned afterward that the winters there are delightful. I like the wh lers in the west and I am planning to go there again in the winter time. The fact was that I had never seen the Saskatchewan river in the winter. I have seen it at other times of the year, when it was in flood and when it was in half-flood. I realize that the Saskatchewan river is not comparable to many other large rivers because its water resources are comparably not as large. But the Almighty has provided enough water to take care of any of the requirements of the three western provinces.
I have seen that river when it was flowing at not less than 100,000 cubic feet per second and when it was flowing at the rate of about
10,000	cubic feet per second. I am referring to the river east of the junction of the two main rivers, the North Saskatchewan, and
Water Conservation

South Saskatchewan. But I had not seen it in the winter time so I visited the river at several points during the winter season, this year. I spent some time examining it at Saskatoon and at Medicine Hat in particular, and I am satisfied that at neither point was the South Saskatchewan flowing at more than 1,500 cubic feet per second, with a maximum of 2,000 cubic feet per second. There is a vast difference between 100,000 cubic feet per second and 2,000 cubic feet per second.
Someone will ask: Where has the water gone to? It has gone down to the sea without having done much good to the parched prairies, which if they are given sufficient water will grow anything. There is no better land in the world. In some places it is a little alkaline, but the, vast proportion of it contains the necessary chemicals to produce crops of all kinds in abundance, provided it gets the water. It is part of my purpose to try to see that it does get that water.
In referring to the flow of the Saskatchewan river I dug up some old tables. I find that in 1915 at Edmonton, during high water, in June that river was flowing 186,600 cubic feet per second, which is a vast volume of water. In that same month the South Saskatchewan was flowing at the rate of 86,000 cubic feet per second at Saskatoon. The low flow of the North Saskatchewan in that year was 700 cubic feet per second, with the South Saskatchewan down to about the same amount.
Our duty is to conserve that water and use it for the irrigation of crops in the west.
In addition to the two other journeys I have referred to, I was considering going to the old country to make a survey into business. I have been there many times, because business is my middle name. I knew that we were considering granting $750,000,000 to help create business over there. I voted for that, and I was in agreement with it. I look upon it as an investment, as an insurance. But I said to myself: That is all very fine, but why should we not spend a few hundred millions in the west to create a home market that would be within our own boundaries? If we could build up the production of farmers, they would make something and be in position to buy from the manufacturers of Canada.
One morning on the way to the house, I believe the second day after the house prorogued, I happened to look at the monument which has been erected just southeast of the east block to the memory of Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and there flashed through my mind what he said when he opened the Saint Andrews locks on the Red River on July 14, 1910. He addressed a great concourse

of people, and I can picture him-a handsome man, with a noble countenance and a fine head of hair. Remembering what he had said I reflected that at the time, he did not see the 2,000 people who were in front of him; he was looking away beyond them, beyond that great body of water which is one of our most splendid lakes-lake Winnipeg. Few people have any conception of its size. It is about 9,400 square miles in area, almost one-third larger than lake Ontario and. only a few hundred square miles smaller than lake Erie. It is next to Great Slave and Great Bear lakes, purely Canadian lakes. I could see him looking down that great lake and saying: This is only the first step in a great vision of transportation right up to the foot of the Rocky mountains. I am not quoting his exact words. He told those people he could see ships coming down 900 miles from Edmonton to that great lake and then right up to the city of Winnipeg. Later I read that he had had the vision to predict something with which I heartily agree and which I hope some day will be carried out. He said that he could see the same boats going up the Winnipeg river to the lake of the Woods along Rainy river, across Rainy lake and then by some means or other to Port Arthur and Fort William.
From 1910 up to the present time all that has been done to carry out that great vision of the then prime minister of this country was a little bit of work done, I believe by Hon. Robert Rogers in 1913. In cooperation with the city of Prince Albert a lock was built in the Prince Albert dam at a point twenty-six miles down the river from the city. That is all that has been done to conserve those waters in the great west. My hon. leader, when premier of Manitoba, projected a grand scheme of damming the Saskatchewan at the east end of Cedar lake and then taking the water through lake Winnipegosis, thence on through lake Manitoba, through lake St. Martin .and then drop into lake Winnipeg, one hundred miles south of Grand, Rapids. That project has this wonderful advantage, that at the point of the drop into lake Winnipeg, 500,000 horse-power could be developed. If the Manitoba government wished to sell that power to anyone who would complete the project, there are plenty of financiers who would say: We will complete it if you will allow us the power. But I believe that large blocks of power like that should belong to the government.
These suggestions have been made in past years, and now we must have action. What I am trying to do now is to encourage the minister, who this year has put into the estim-

Water Conservation
ates a vote of $10,060,000. I should like to see a similar vote put in the estimates for each of the next nine years; make it a ten-year programme of spending $10,000,000 a year, or $100,000,000 in the ten years. I do not say that I want to see the minister there that long, sir, but whoever the minister might happen to be would carry out any plans instituted now. Such a ten-year programme would enable us to complete this' project for the conservation of water and the construction of irrigation works. That amount would not, of course, create power to the extent that it could be created, nor permit of the canalization of the two branches of the river. That would take much more money, but it is one which should be carried out. Perhaps that will be a project for the future.
We have some fine examples of what can be done. What did the late great president of the United States, President Roosevelt, do in 1933? From his boyhood he had heard of the possibilities of conservation of the waters of the Tennessee river, just as the western members must have heard from their boyhood of plans to conserve western waters which have never been carried out. The conservation of the waters of the Tennessee river was first projected in 1807. After President Roosevelt took office he said, in 1933, that that was long enough to wait, and he went ahead, and in twelve years had revolutionized the economy of seven states. He canalized that great river, built nine large dams on the main river, as well as many other dams, and to-day they have a navigable route from Paducah at the month of the river right up to Knoxville, 650 miles away. Last year that river transported
150,000,000 ton-miles of freight. What has been accomplished down there is stupendous. They produced from that river the greatest single aggregation of power, not in any one place, but from any one river that is to be found the world over, developing from three and a half million to four million horsepower. What that has done to restore the economy of all the cities in that river valley is something the whole world can be proud of. We can do the same thing in the Saskatchewan river valley. When I think of what those people out there in our westren country have endured I am almost ashamed that in the past I did not take the part that I am taking now. I am not going to let up now; I am going to keep at it until I see this, thing finished-the restoration of the economy of the west. I know it can be done-and all these projects are self-liquidating.
I have made a careful survey of irrigation in many states, covering many thousands of
miles. If any one goes out to the west and crosses the international boundary line into the United States and goes through Montana, Idaho, the valley of California, Arizona, Utah, and part of Oregon, what will you see? You will see the marvellous transformation that has been brought about in the last fifteen years. They reclaimed 3,000,000 acres of land from the dried-out desert, so dry . that it would not even grow cactus, and you never saw such bountiful production as you can see there to-day. In Idaho they have land producing 750 bags of potatoes to the acre and 1,000 bags of onions, and all the other crops are in proportion. We can do the same thing in Alberta and Saskatchewan if only we give our land water; and we can give it water, because the Saskatchewan river, if conserved, will provide all the water that the west can use in all the projects that we have in mind, and will provide irrigation, power, navigation and anything else that will help to make that country grow.
Let me show you how the people in the east will profit from the carrying out of this project-because I cannot separate it from the east. The east must come forward, its business men, its bankers and financial men because the east will receive just as much in the way of returns, Mr. Speaker, as will the western farmers. The western states, from those 3,000,000 acres of reclaimed land, produced $400,000,000 of products for the states themselves, and in addition vast sums of money were obtained through processing those products and sending them to the east. Every year there went to the east $200,000,000 worth of orders for manufactured products. That is how the east will benefit if we reclaim these
3,000,000 acres in our Canadian west, and so the eastern manufacturer and the eastern banker will get their return just the same as the western farmer. We want unity in Canada, which we all love, and there is nothing that would do so much to bring about unity in this country as carrying out this project. I often used to sit in this house and listen to the western members advocating such projects in past years. None of them are here to-day, except perhaps the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine). They advocated them then, and I did not seem to know enough to understand it. But I understand now, sir, from much travel in the west. I know what the reclamation of that land would mean, what magnificent returns there would be all along the line, what a bountiful thing it would be for all of Canada, and not merely for western economy. This whole project has been a football long enough. I have read everything that I could on it-from Dan to Beersheba, I was going to say, but that would hardly be appropriate.

Yes, and I find that back in 1804 the XY company, a fur company, which 'had branches in the west long before there was any settlement at all, wrote to their principals' that tlhe west would never come into its own until water from the South Saskatchewan river was sent over the dried-out parts of tlie prairies. The father of the late General McDonald, of the pension board until his death a few years ago, was a Hudson's Bay factor at what was then Fort Ellice, at the junction of the Assiniboine and Qu'Appelle rivers. Away back in 1854 he recommended such a project, and from that day to this all that I have been able to read of engineers' reports has recommended the same thing. In heaven's name when are we going to carry out some of these things?
I know that the minister is having a survey made on the South Saskatchewan river to find a place to build a dam, and I give him credit for it. Of course you have to have something solid on which to build a dam. I presume that the minister has not yet received a report from his engineers that they have found a solid place somewhere near River-hurst. But they will find it, and if they do not find it they can build dams as was done on the Tennessee, with bases half a mile wide and with the regular core that the engineers use. I understand that dam sites have been found at two other places. I have here a core taken from the bottom of the St. Mary's river, and I am glad to say that I have had word lately that they are now about ready to call for tenders for the building of that dam. The building of a dam on the St. Mary's would mean the reclamation of 300,000 acres south of the Saskatchewan river. I have also a core obtained from the Red Deer. Near Buffalo lake a great dam could be built, which would mean the reclamation of 500,000 acres between Buffalo lake and Stettler on the north and Hanna and Youngstown and Acadia on the south. There is no reason why a project could not be undertaken immediately across the Bow river to reclaim all that area of Redcliff, Ronalane and Medicine Hat.
This winter I made an examination of that district, even in the midst of the snow, and that would mean another 300,000 acres. From Saskatoon west to Rosetown, and further down to Kindersley, there is an area of another
1,000,000 acres waiting to be reclaimed, if we can get the dam site on the South Saskatchewan river; and there are 1,000,000 acres east of the South Saskatchewan river as far as Estevan.

Here is a programme which the minister, I submit, ought to carry out to the full. I am prepared to encourage him with all the strength I have. I would support him in this effort to put through a $10,000,000 vote this year, and I would suggest that he come back next year, if he is still minister, and ask for another ten millions, and another the year after that. As long as he is minister he should ask for ten millions every year until we get the whole project completed so that we may reclaim the dried-out areas in the prairie provinces and restore the economy of the people there, and give them that chance to which they are entitled. They were put there on lands by the government-not by this government particularly, but by all governments-and they have been trying to eke out an existence on land that does not always produce a crop.
I should like to read a few words written by that distinguished man. Mr. R. O. Sweezey, with regard to the western projects and their importance. If I might be allowed to put it on Hansard without reading it, it would save time.

speechtext:
With the consent of the house I will hand it to Hansard:
There is an area of some thirty million acres of farm land comprised within the southern parts of the three prairie provinces which is subject to such adverse conditions, caused by lack of moisture, that when sown to wheat the chances are proven to be about four to one against the farmer reaping better than one-half the crop that his labour and the quality of his land would entitle him to. Frequently he loses an entire year through complete crop failure. With wheat he has an occasional bit of luck, but it is rarely more than a bit, and, because of the arid conditions, experience shows that wheat is the only product that may in a measure survive a season's distressful drought. Too often, though, the failure has been complete, and so the mental anguish and human distress has been piling up to the breaking point. At one time the ground water level was higher, and it often sufficed to bring a crop to maturity. But the gradual lowering of the ground water level since the first breaking of the sod is responsible for the growing severity that has led to what now constitutes an utterly intolerable situation.
The problem is now a national one, and bids fair to be calamitous unless responsibility and leadership is assumed by someone for the purpose of applying the obvious remedies of simple engineering practice. Unfortunately, however, economists, financial experts and political scientists have not been keeping pace with the progress of engineering and science. So, when a large, though simple, project of this nature looms up, it is usually procrastinated to its doom.

Water Conservation
Saving the losses from one or two years would easily provide all the means for remedial works to permanently cure the evil. From a financial viewpoint it would be the most profitable project ever attempted in this country. As a self-liquidating enterprise it merits the most attentive study of statesmen. Private capital is ready and willing to assume responsibility for rescuing the western prairies from their heartbreaking losses.
There is one other item that I would refer to, Mr. Speaker, and it is of such vital and transcendant importance that I would hesitate to omit it. I refer to the water supply of Moose Jaw and Regina, two beautiful cities. I have here some clippings from the Regina Leader Post and the Times of Moose Jaw. I will read only one item, though I could quote extensively to the same effect, because there are a number of items of the same purport. Under date March 5, 1946 there appeared the following item:
At noon yesterday there were three feet ten inches of water in the reservoir representing
190.000	gallons.
That is only one out of many items indicating the same thing. Now I say, Mr. Speaker, that we in this House of Commons, all of us without exception, stand condemned unless we do our utmost to give to the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina the means of defence against fire. We all saw recently what happened across the river here in Hull, when that woodpile was burning. It contained only
16.000	cords of pulpwood, and yet what a flame it made. How much water do you think was required to put it out? Yesterday I was talking to the chief engineer of the Hull fire department, Mr. Lanctot, and I wish to congratulate him and all his captains and the men serving under him on the wonderful job they did in saving the paper mill over there. I did not believe it was possible; but to do it they had to pour 62,000,000 gallons of water on that fire.
What would happen in Moose Jaw to-day with less than a million and a half gallons and Regina with less than five million gallons per day? They have no water to spare. Their plight would be tragic. We will stand in the light of public condemnation unless we make every effort to see that this dam is built on the south Saskatchewan river in order to provide the people of those cities with the water they so badly need. I hate to think what would happen if a fire one-tenth the size of the Hull fire started at the west end of Moose Jaw or the west end of Regina, with a wind blowing from the west. What do you think would happen to those two fine cities?
As a member of this house I would hold myself condemned unless I raised my voice and did my part to encourage the minister and to support him in any measure that is required to speed up the construction of the dam on the South Saskatchewan river near Riverhurst. The work should be proceeded with as rapidly as possible so as to provide the people of those two prairie cities with an ample water supply, apart from irrigation.
When I was in Moose Jaw I visited different factories, and I was greatly interested in one that was operated by a man from Czechoslovakia, I believe. In that factory they were making glucose from wheat, and that is something that the west is just built for. The gentleman who was with me was from the waterworks department of Moose Jaw and he told the proprietor that he would have to cut down on his use of water. The proprietor assured him that as it was he could not get enough water to fill the orders he had. When I heard that, I felt that I too would be condemned if I did not bring this matter up in the house. Those people have an opportunity to run ten factories instead of one, producing something that Canada needs. Their product is shipped east, and my good friend who represents London tells me that he buys a good deal of it himself. I want to do everything I can to stir up this house and the west, as well as the financial and business men of the east, so that we may all get behind the government and help the minister to carry through a project which will conserve water all along the Saskatchewan river, to reforest the foothills of the rockies, and to assist the Alberta government in preventing further fires. I would feel like reproaching myself if I did not speak as I am doing this afternoon.
I am going to put a map in each member's post office box. It is a composite map which I drew myself. In this connection I should like to say a word about Major Duncan Stuart, K.C., a wonderful old man who is well known to my hon. friend the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I take off my hat to him, because I found his map helpful. The same can be said of his articles on irrigation. In these articles he points out, as I have pointed out, that the whole programme is self-liquidating. Although it might cost $200 millions to complete the whole job in reality it would not cost the country a single dollar, because every dollar would be returned in crops alone apart from power. Then later on there would be taxes coming in. This is a permanent programme. It is not a programme where we put money in and never get it back. It is not that kind of

Water Conservation
programme; it is a Canada programme, a Canadian market programme, a self-liquidating programme giving thousands and thousands of jobs. Moreover it will create forty thousand new farms and provide orders for the equipment for those new farms. There will be about eighty irrigated acres to the farm.
One only has to go into southern Alberta, where we have a little irrigation, to see the wonderfpl results that can be obtained. I think of the fine city of Lethbridge, which went over the top in the three last victory loans, first in all Canada. Why? Because round about they have about 600,000 acres of irrigated land, taking in Taber, Cardston and Raymond and many other fine villages and towns. There is nothing that will give the same returns as a programme of this kind, and in the long run it will not cost the country a dollar.
