speechtext:
I am glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) say that some work has been going on for the last seven or eight years. I think that is true, but I rose particularly to support, the resolution of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). Had I been drawing the resolution I might have drawn it in slightly different terms, but its intent is such that I think eveiy hon. member of the house can support it. I and those associated with me-and I have no doubt that I am speaking now for others who come from western Canada-are very pleased that the hon. member for Davenport, representing as he does a city constituency in eastern Canada, has felt it incumbent upon himself to bring this matter up in the house at this time.
As the hon. member said in the course of his remarks, the question has been discussed in the house on many occasions in the past,

Water Conservation
but without a great deal of success. We understand, of course, that action in these matters, involving, as they do in the final analysis, probably several hundred million dollars, takes some time, particularly when it appears that only one area of the country is interested. But the hon. member placed another complexion upon it this afternoon; he has shown clearly that to undertake work of this kind is in the interest not only of the prairie provinces but of the whole economy of Canada, and that upon the prosperity of that great area which we call the prairies depends in no small measure the prosperity of the great industrial centres of all of Canada.
I was interested when the hon. member told us about the various projects that he has visited in the United States, because over the last twenty years I myself have had the privilege of seeing many of them. In 1938, driving back from Los Angeles to Ottawa in the autumn of the year, I stayed in a little town called Needles in Arizona. I was told that there were twenty-seven motorboats in that little town-twenty-seven motorboats in the middle of the desert. The nearest water, except for the dried out Colorado river, was some 130 or 140 miles away. I was told that when the dam 120 or 130 miles south of .the little town of Needles, Arizona, was completed, there would be a lake extending all the way to this town, which wpuld be a little port and the motorboats could then be used. The same thing occurred in Montana. I visited Fort Peck before the dam was completed in Montana. I was told that a lake would be made on the Missouri river which would have a shoreline-I am speaking from memory now- of 1,628 miles. From that scheme, which was mainly a power and flood control project, there could be irrigated a great deal of land.
I have seen the developments in the state of Washington, where they proposed to use the water from Coulee dam so that it would flow once more through the Dry Falls and irrigate an area which was, when I saw it, nothing but an arid, barren desert with a little sage bush on it. I remember being told that
200,000	families would be established in that area in the state of Washington. One could mention the other great projects in the United States and elsewhere across the world; and when I think of the water which flows down the two Saskatchewans, which runs down the Red Deer river into the South Saskatchewan and into other rivers flowing south into Montana, I realize what we could do with that fertile land in the southern part of the prairie provinces if only we had that inch of water 63260-41J
in June and that inch of water in July that would ensure always something of a crop over the irrigated area.
In 1938 I had the privilege of introducing into this house a resolution which was supported by the hon. member for Davenport. While it was debated, it was more or less brushed off. The expense was too great; the undertaking was too large, and after all, the rains would come again. I moved the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should place before parliament at an early date plans, or proposals, for a comprehensive and authoritative survey of water conservation, irrigation possibilities, and other feasible projects for the permanent rehabilitation of the drought-stricken area of western Canada and its people.
Those of us who lived in that area then knew that the resolution placed before the house the need of the people at that time. It was a drought-stricken area. In 1938 the prairies were just emerging from the worst period in their history since the first settlement of the southern plains. I remember that in preparing to speak on the resolution I went into the library and gathered together everything I could find about the prairies in the days gone by. I remember reading the report of Captain Palliser, who made his trip through southern Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1858. I quoted from that report in 1938; I do not propose to quote from it now, but I recall that he spoke of the desolated plains and the desert cactus which grew in what is now southwestern Saskatchewan and southeastern Alberta, after he had left what he described as-and these are his exact words- "the creek where the bones lie." I have no doubt that "the creek where the bones lie" was the site of the city in which my hon. friend from Calgary west (Mr. Smith) was born, and in which I had the privilege of living for a good many years; that is, Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan. At that time Captain Palliser, as those of you who have read the report will remember, described all the country which lay west and south of the Qu'Appelle valley and the South Saskatchewan river as an arid plain where nothing grew. He spoke of a place he named The Elbow, where he met a band of Indians who warned him that if he was going in a southwesterly direction he had better take not only food for himself but fodder for the horses and even sticks with which to make fires, because he would find nothing in that country either to eat or to burn.
We saw something of that in the thirties. Not one of us who lived in western Canada
<344
Water Conservation

during that period will ever forget the misery of those ten years; the days when we drove over the prairies and could not see the radiator caps on our automobiles because of dust; when in the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw we drove with our headlights full on day after day in order that we might see in the darkness caused by the 'blowing of the topsoil of that rich prairie land. It is true, of course, that a remarkable comeback has been made in the last six or seven years. We bad hoped this would occur, and it has occurred. But we know from the historic past that these prolonged droughts in western Canada are periodic. It is proved by history. If you cut down the trees and look at the rings, they tell the story of the periodic dry and wet years during the time of their growth, which is perhaps a hundred years or more in the case of the elm trees that grow in some of our valleys. We know that country is subject to periodic and devastating drought. What it has meant to the men and women of those plains no financial balance sheet can ever tell; the misery, the dread, the piling up of debt, the women living alone in prairie homes who day after day heard the winds blow and saw the dust sweeping by the house, with nothing growing on the land year after year. Many of them, and it cannot be wondered at, even lost their reason as a result of the conditions under which they lived. And in this country, east and west, we spent millions and millions of dollars in relief. I am not going. to complain, because the people of eastern Canada came to the rescue of the people who lived on the plains. They sent us carloads of vegetables, of food and of clothing, and this parliament appropriated millions of dollars for the relief of man and beast. And when it was all over, after the low level of relief upon which people were compelled to live, what had Canada to show for what had been done? Nothing but a people who still hoped that the rains might come and the land might once .again be productive.
As the hon. member for Davenport has said, the cause of the drought in western Canada can be explained in only one way, the lack of moisture in the soil. Yet when that lack of moisture was clearly before us and the rains were, scant or came not at all, millions and millions of gallons of water were flowing through those plains in the various rivers, which might have been utilized to relieve at least in part the tragic conditions with which we were confronted. And let us remember that in a period of drought the dry soil blows, and wind erosion is added to the disastrous consequences of the lack of moisture. I remember a constituent of mine writing to me in 1937;

I have the letter in my office even now. He lived quite close to the South Saskatchewan river, near Saskatchewan Landing, just north of Swift Current. He said, "I have been sitting to-day on the bank of the Saskatchewan. All the valley up from the Landing, through Kyle and Tuberose right up to Elrose and Rose-town, is a scene of devastation; nothing grows. Yet to-day I see the Saskatchewan river in flood." That was in July, the flood period. He went on to say, "The river is lower, than it sometimes is at this period, yet millions of gallons of water are going by which might be used to relieve the drought on the farms of this locality." ,
Like the hon. member for Davenport, at that time I discussed irrigation with the best engineers I knew. I went carefully over the contour maps of the dried out area, and as a layman I would say that widespread irrigation does not present insuperable difficulties, particularly on the northern side of the Mis-souri-Coteau divide, which of course is in part the southern side or Canadian base of the Pal-liser triangle. As -we have been told this afternoon, the problem is the conservation of waters in the rivers which flow together and form the South Saskatchewan river-that is, the Red Deer and the other tributaries-and the impounding of that water in a series of dams in the deep river valleys or in the mountains. I believe, as my hon. friend says, that the impounding of water near Riverhurst and the utilization of that water by the building of channels along natural lines of flow, as the contour maps indicate, would carry water down to Moose Jaw and Regina-yes, and even beyond Moose Jaw and Regina, down to the Souris river near Weyburn and into the Souris river valley right through Estevan and beyond. The contour maps clearly indicate that this is not an insoluble problem; it can be done. I believe the physical difficulties can be overcome. Of course, as my hon. friend has said, a by-product of an irrigation project of this description would be the generating of comparatively cheap power, which could be used for the rural electrification so badly needed in the western provinces, where there is so little of it.
Many people conceive of irrigation channels as long straight cuts, like a chess-board. But that is not what irrigation might be. As I suggest, it might follow the natural channels and contour. There are depressions running north and south, east and west, through which water might be channelled. While I appreciate what the Minister of Agriculture and the government have done in connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act- and if I may say so, as a westerner, J believe

Water Conservation
one of the best projects ever undertaken by a government in Canada was that which is called the P.F.R.A. project-still, they have not been extensive enough. There are still a good many coulees, still a good many valleys, which could be dammed to conserve the spring run-off. They would carry not only the water from the rivers, but the run-offs from the land after the winter snows have melted. For instance, we had a large quantity of snow in the prairie provinces this winter. This spring, when the snow melted, it ran down the coulees, found the channels, and away it went to the rivers and out to the sea. Those coulees might be dammed and the water conserved so that at least farms in the neighbourhood would have hay and be able to grow vegetables. In the event of a dry season they would at least have something upon which they could rely for food, both for man and for beast.
I have been told by engineers that with proper conservation in the mountains, and with appropriate dams placed at intervals on the South Saskatchewan from where the Red Deer joins it in Alberta, to a point south of Saskatoon, sufficient water could be impounded to give needed moisture to a very large area of central and southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. I say of course that I have been told this. I do not profess to be an expert in irrigation or in engineering. Every man to his own trade. But I believe that a thorough investigation by those who are competent to make an appraisal would indicate that a great deal can be done in this regard.
I have always been in favour of a really authoritative and comprehensive survey of these irrigation possibilities. I have heard the objection raised that a project of this description would cost hundreds of millions of dollars. I noticed that this afternoon the hon. member for Davenport mentioned $100 million. Well, what is $100 million, after all? We spent more than $100 million on the very lorv relief levels upon which we maintained people in western Canada during those eight or nine years of terrible drought. We spent more than that. The highest estimate I have heard for damming the rivers in the mountains and for making the necessary channels to convey the water here and there, to build conservation dams and undertake a comprehensive irrigation project for the whole of the southern prairie provinces is S400 million. Yes, $400 million is a lot of money. But let me point out that it is less than we spent in one month for the prosecution of the war.
That large amount of money was only one month's war expenditures-and I am purposely citing the largest figure I have heard
mentioned, because I do not think that amount of money would have to be expended. Let me emphasize the fact that to ensure life and opportunity in a vast area of this country an amount less than one month's war expenditures might be required. When we realize that this expenditure would make a great country permanently productive and give possibilities of increased prosperity, not only to the people who inhabit that country but to the whole of the Dominion of Canada, we can see that the amount involved is relatively small. As I have already said, during the years of drought, when the rains failed to come to us in western Canada, we spent from a quarter to a half that amount in unproductive relief.
Inevitably, from the history of the country as we know it, droughts will come again, and they may even be more prolonged than the one we experienced between 1930 and 1940. The Indians who have inhabited the- plains throughout the years talk about lakes being dried up, although they are not now dried up. In the constituency of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is a body of water known as Long Lake. Long ago I was told by the Indians that seventy or eighty years ago, when they were children, Long Lake was so dry that they could drive across it in a wagon. Consequently we know that there can be even more prolonged droughts than those which we have experienced.
The hon. member for Davenport has mentioned what irrigation has brought to one part of the prairies. Those of us who have seen the irrigation in southern Alberta, around Lethbridge, realize the truth of the statement that is has done much for that country. One day a year ago last July I was in Medicine Hat. It was a hot day, and very dry. A friend of mine was to drive me to Lethbridge. We drove from Medicine Hat across a scorched plain, where the oats and wheat, stapding five or six inches high, and headed out, were dry and dead. Then, all of a sudden, the wind being from the west, we could smell the odour of vegetation; and when we arrived at Taber, Alberta, the limit of the irrigation project, we passed into a country which was a veritable paradise. The corn was standing high and green, the grain waving in the wind, acres and acres of sugar beets-land that was a picture not only of beauty but of productivity. And all this because there was water: water which the other parts of the prairies with exactly the same kind of soil- just as productive, if given the opportunity, but without that one essential-did not have. And when we got to where there was water,
Water Conservation

brought in by the cunning and ingenuity of man, we saw how productive that soil really could be.
We do not need to go to the Sudan; we do not need to go to India; we do not need to go to the places that have been mentioned

Arizona, Montana, or Washington; we do not need to go to any of those .places to see what water does for what would otherwise be an arid area. All we have to do is to take a drive into southern Alberta during a hot. dry summer, and we can see in our own country how prairie land has been transformed under irrigation.
This party to whicn i Delong has always urged these irrigation projects, both provincially and1 federally. As my hon. friend has said, navigable -waters are under the control of the federal authorities. As my hon. friend said also, the people who settled in these areas were settled there by the authority of the parliament of Canada. As far as southwestern Saskatchewan and southeastern Alberta are concerned, I can remember that there was strong opposition from persons who were living in those areas and who knew that without irrigation people who went in there to settle would be doomed to disappointment in the days to come. Sir Frederick Haultain, the head of the territorial government of the northwest territories until the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were formed, warned against the possibilities of drought. Many others, including myself, did not accept the reasons given by the ranchers in the Medicine Hat area for opposing the settlement of that land. We were under the impression that the ranchers were a little selfish, that they were trying to keep the land from settlement in order to retain their ranching leases. But time has proved that they were right and we were wrong, that the settlement of that country was ill-advised from the point of view of agriculture.
It is true there was a good crop in that area in 1915 and another in 1942, with a few fair crops in between. But without irrigation, much of that Medicine Hat and Swift Current country, as well as other parts _of the country between there and Moose Jaw and Regina and to the south, cannot be made productive year after year. Ways and means must first be found of getting moisture to the land. As I said, we have always been in favour of it. In February, 1938, I moved a resolution in this house, and at the same time the C.C.F. group in the legislature at Regina moved the following resolution:
That this assembly respectifully request the federal government to set aside an appropriation of at least $50,000,000 this year, to be used in 
investigation and completion of feasible water conservation, irrigation and other projects, directed towards the permanent rehabilitation of the drought area of this province.
That was not a partisan resolution. None of these resolutions were partisan. At that time the government in power in Saskatchewan was a Liberal government. While they did not approve the amount suggested in the resolution, and amended it, the amended resolution which called for a study of irrigation projects in that part of Canada was passed unanimously. The matter transcends the needs of the various provinces. It is the responsibility of all Canada. It is a work of importance to the whole of our country.
I' do not want to prolong the discussion, because many hon. members who come from other parts of the prairie land as -well as other parts of Canada will wish to participate in the debate. A few days ago we were discussing immigration. Whatever we may think of immigration, whether we believe in wholesale immigration, as some do and as I do not, whether we believe in planned immigration, by which people would be brought in and settled where they should' be settled under proper conditions, where they can be given the opportunities they should be given; whether we believe that they should not be brought in in indigestible numbers, the fact remains that there is room for many thousands of people in this country. I cannot think of any part of Canada which offers greater possibility of better homes, better climate and better living conditions than the prairie land, provided a certain amount of stability is assured in the production of crops. Give the prairie land moisture, and the prairie land will produce crops.
The other day I looked up the debates of 1938 and I found that at that time some took the view that if we irrigated we would increase our production so tremendously that we would not be able to find markets. We already had surpluses on our hands, in spite of the drought years through which we had been passing. All I can say is that it is a strange world where there is starvation or near starvation on almost every hand and yet the production of foodstuffs is discouraged.
I referred the other evening to the privilege I had had of being on the social economic council at San Francisco, when the nations of the world1 obligated themselves to see to it that as far as possible everybody every day in the year should have an opportunity of eating a decent meal. There ought never to be a fear of overproduction in our country. We do have great crops, and perhaps sometimes we cannot

Water Conservation
find immediate export markets, but any surplus should be regarded as a reserve against the time when crops may fail.
I speak not only for myself but those in this party with whom I am associated when I say that we are in favour of a comprehensive investigation into the possibilities, not merely of a series of small irrigation projects but of a comprehensive irrigation project to make the prairie land productive year after year and to guarantee to the people who live there the opportunity of producing from their labours year after year, indeed an opportunity for this country to become more prosperous than it has been in the past.
We support the idea behind the resolution of the hon. member for Davenport. We are grateful that he has introduced this resolution. He sits for an eastern constituency, and perhaps is thus able to render greater service to the area we are discussing than those of us can who have been introducing such resolutions in the past, for he can have no selfish interest in the matter.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO QUESTIONS AFFECTING SASKATCHEWAN RIVER WATERSHED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) on the campaign he has consistently waged in this country in the interests of water conservation and irrigation in western Canada. The work he has done in the past and the work he is doing to-day is greatly appreciated by all the people in western Canada. I am sure all the people in the west will appreciate the importance of the resolution he has submitted to this house, which reads in part:	'
. . . to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river.
Forest fires and logging operations have caused a great deal of devastation on this watershed. The task of conserving this watershed in the past has been largely the responsibility of Alberta, but of course it is too large a job for any one province. It is a large job; it is a costly job. The whole dominion is vitally interested in seeing that this work is carried out efficiently, because the waters from the watershed flow not merely through Alberta but down through Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and these provinces will need every drop of water that can be conserved in those rivers for irrigation, stock watering, power development and human consumption in the future.
Again, eastern Canada has a direct interest in that work being carried out because, when the west prospers, eastern Canada benefits by an expansion of markets and sales in the west. In this house we have heard a great deal about the St. Mary's river project, the development at Medicine Hat, and certain developments from rivers in Saskatchewan-all worth-while projects; but we have not heard very much about the utilization of waters from this watershed in the east central part of Alberta, and I should like to speak of this for a few moments.
I think most members of the house remember that great engineer by the name of William Pearce and his great scheme for that area, mainly for the purposes of stock watering. Under that project it would have been possible to water between 17,000,000 and 18.000.000 acres. I do not mean by that irrigation, but it would have brought water to pasture lands of that acreage. In 1922-23, government engineers made a survey based upon the William Pearce project and as a result of this survey a scheme was developed known as the North Saskatchewan irrigation project, which would have irrigated approximately 1,000,000 acres in Saskatchewan and
500,000	acres in Alberta. The cost would have been around $100,000,000. The essentia! difference between the William Pearce project and the North Saskatchewan project was that the William Pearce scheme was a stock watering project, while the North Saskatchewan was an irrigation project. The mechanics of the two were very similar. They both proposed to divert water from the North Saskatchewan river and the Clearwater river down Raven river into the Red Deer river and to place a dam about fifty feet high below the junction with the Red Deer. Then it would have been possible to divert water by gravity from that dam through a canal 146 miles long to Sullivan lake, which would have provided a storage of 1,500,000 acre feet. From Sullivan lake it would have been possible to irrigate 500,000 acres, and water would also have been carried by a gravity canal and by natural waterways, namely, Sounding creek and Eyehill creek to Tramping lake in Saskatchewan, and from Tramping lake 1,000.000 acres could have been irrigated. However, that project was by many people considered impracticable, mainly because there would have been a heavy seepage of water and heavy evaporation from Sullivan lake to Tramping lake because of the sandy nature of the soil.
Another thing that weighed against the project was its actual size. It was a large one costing $100,000,000. During the war that
Water Conservation

did not sound very much, but in those days it appeared to be an astronomical figure, and unfortunately there is a tendency now in some places to revert to those pre-war ideas on questions of expenditure.
Many additional surveys have been made since that time. A number of surveys were made from 1938 to 1940 by P.F.R.A. engineers, and I pay tribute to the fine work they have done in conducting these surveys and surveys for smaller projects. The surveys made from 1938 to 1940 were surveys with a view to providing not merely for irrigation but for power development purposes. The cost of irrigation would have been considerably higher finder those projects because it was proposed to pump the water instead of having it moved by gravity. They also proposed to obtain power from the Calgary Power Company at a time when they were pumping water heavily and to make the power available to the Calgary Power Company in winter time.
As a result of all these surveys and the promises made, particularly at election time, it was only natural that the people in that area became very much interested in irrigation, and a great deal of pressure has been exerted from time to time on the government to start work on one of these projects. The people in that area are hoping that the government will finally decide which project would be of greatest advantage to the people and start construction thereon immediately. However, a good deal of opposition developed to the idea of diverting water from the North Saskatchewan and the Clearwater rivers into the Red Deer river, because it was felt that the water might be needed lower down the river in Saskatchewan, and therefore new surveys were made of a project which would irrigate a limited number of acres in Alberta, utilizing the waters of the Red Deer river alone, instead of diverting the water from the North Saskatchewan river.
A brief outline of the new scheme known as the Red Deer diversion project, which was referred to by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon, is as follows: Tt is proposed to place a dam on the Red Deer river just above the content bridge and build up the water to a height of 150 feet. That dam would be approximately thirty miles east of the town of Red Deer. Then by gravity canal the water would be carried to Hamilton lake, which is at a lower level than Sullivan lake, a distance of from sixty-five to seventy miles. At Hamilton lake it would be possible to provide a maximum storage of 380,000 acre feet, and additional storage could be provided in a number of lakes surrounding Hamilton lake, one of

them being Kirkpatrick lake. From these reservoirs it is proposed to irrigate about half a million acres. Actually in that area there are over 900,000 acres that could be irrigated, but the waters from the Red Deer river will only be sufficient to irrigate half a million acres. If, later on, it was possible to use waters from the North Saskatchewan river, using 2,000 cubic feet per second, it would be possible to irrigate another 400,000 acres. But that is not included in the scheme. The Red Deer river diversion provides only for the irrigation of half a million acres, using the waters of the Red Deer river alone. Under this scheme 1,200 miles of waterways could be re-watered, and on the basis that range lands benefit for a distance of three miles from live water, 8,000,000 acres of pasture land would be available under this scheme.
Some of the main advantages of the Red Deer river diversion scheme over other schemes are as follows. In the first place it is the most northerly scheme of its size to be found anywhere in the world, and for that reason there would be less evaporation than there would be on other projects farther south; also the water is carried by gravity, which costs considerably less than pumping the water. Perhaps one of the most important factors in this scheme is that substantial services have already been established in that area, and therefore it would be better to go ahead with it than with projects in some new district where there are no such services. We have in that area two railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, running east and west, and with branch lines running north and south; we have two main highways running east and west, and two highways running north and south; substantial telephone service has also been established, and there are five hospitals in that area. The question of population throughout that area is a tragic one, and in that connection I should like to read from a report tabled in this house on September 10 of last year from P.F.R.A., which has this to say regarding the Red Deer river diversion scheme.
It will provide settlement, permanent homes and means of livelihood for 7,500 families in a section of western Canada from which over 90 per cent of the original settlers were forced by drought: it resettles an area now practically depopulated; the area will support between
30,000	and 40.000 people. It will provide irrigation for approximately 500,000 acres of land suitable for irrigation. This land is not now in production and is largely publicly-owned. It will rehabilitate 24 urban communities now practically depopulated from the years of drought.

Water Conservation
Then regarding labour requirements:
Estimated labour requirements:	The actual
construction of the works will employ 1,500 men steadily for eighteen months. This does not include indirect labour required in the preparation of materials, cement, lumber, equipment and miscellaneous supplies, nor that required in servicing the purchasing power of these men and their families.
The area to which I have referred lies within a square of approximately 7,000 square miles. It is bounded on the south by the Red Deer river, on the east by the Saskatchewan boundary, on the north by a line running east and west through the town of Castor, south of township 38, and on the west by a line running north and south through the town of Hanna in range 14. This area was settled chiefly between the years 1909 and 1918. Settlement at that time was encouraged by colonization companies, railway companies and certain government officials, and that encouragement was given in spite of the fact that the government had been warned time and again by prominent engineers that that land was not suitable for settlement.
For instance, reference has been made to Captain Palliser, who, in 1860, warned that a certain area within the so-called Palliser triangle was not suitable for settlement. It is true that a great deal of the land in that triangle has proved satisfactory, but on the other hand the record of the land lying in the south central part of the triangle fully substantiates the warnings issued by Captain Palliser at that time. That includes the area to which I am referring to-day.
In addition to Palliser, we had warnings from a number of men such as Doctor Hector, Professor John Macoun and Professor James Mavor. Warnings were issued from time to time by various engineers and surveyors who had been working through that area from 1870 on until the time of settlement in 1909.
The consequences of settlement in that area have been extremely tragic, as shown in the report from which I have just quoted, when it says that over ninety per cent of the population had to move out owing to drought. The effects of droughts were not as devastating in the earlier days of settlement because in the first place there were fairly heavy rains in 1915 and 1916, and unfortunately the crops grown during those two years encouraged more people to come in. Moreover, there was plenty of range land. The land had not been fenced and the farmers were able to run their stock on the open range instead of confining it to half-section areas such as they may have obtained from the dominion government. In 63260-42
addition to that, there was an almost unlimited amount of work available for the farmers, who could work on their land for a certain length of time and then go and work on the construction of branch railway lines that were being constructed at that time through those areas.
However, conditions changed rapidly. Continued drought and soil drifting made it impossible for many farmers to continue to farm their land,, because as soon as they started to cultivate it the dry winds began to blow the land away. As soon as farmers fenced their farms off in half-section lots they found that, owing to the dryness of the land, it took over forty acres of pasture to feed one head of stock. Of course a man with 320 acres cannot carry many head of stock if the land can pasture only one head to forty acres. Eight head of stock would not provide a living for any man, so that these farmers could not make a living out of live stock when they had only 320 acres of dry land to pasture them on.
The situation that developed in that area is graphically illustrated in a report on the rehabilitation of the drought areas of Alberta, issued in 1935 by the Department of Agriculture. This shows what happened in that area during those years:
With the coming of the railways, settlement poured into the short grass plains. From 1911 onward, the rancher who had previously occupied this area was progressively crowded out, and by 1920 settlement was almost complete. Bumper crops and high prices in 1915 and 1916, had removed the last remaining misgivings on the part of those who were afraid of the short grass plains. Roads, telephones, schools, churches and social services of all kinds were demanded and provided-the - whole superstructure, literally built on stalks of gold and wheat, in a foundation of shifting sand. Then came 1917, 1918, 1921 and 1922-drought, discouragement and despair-the covered wagon and the settler on the move again like wild geese in the spring going north. Another lease of life, good crops in 1926, 1927 and 1928-then drought again, followed by wholesale abandonment-40 per cent, 50 per cent, 60 per cent, and 80 per cent in some districts. The burden of taxation necessary to maintain necessary services bearing heavier and heavier on the settlers who remained. Finally it became difficult to operate schools, to maintain roads. Telephone lines were abandoned by the hundreds of miles. Life became more primitive and intolerable through lack of natural community life. Such is the history of the greater portion of Palliser's triangle-one of the greatest mistakes that national policy ever made.
As a consequence of so many farmers leaving that area, the rest of the farmers who remained were able to make a better living because they had more land upon which to run their stock, though I wcdfl again point out

Water Conservation

that when it takes forty acres to pasture one head of stock a man would need to have from 2,000 to 3,000 acres to carry fifty or sixty head of stock if he wanted to make a decent living. As pointed out in that report, the history of the whole area has been a tragic one. People came to the district in their youth full of ambition and hope for the future, some with a small amount of capital, although, generally speaking, they did not bring much capital with them. They slaved and toiled for many years. They cleared the rocks away and broke the sod, only to see the land blow away in dust storms and the soil drifted up under the fences; and as they fenced their pastures and the grass was eaten down to the ground, the stock began to eat right down into the roots. The result was that even pasture land, never cultivated, started to drift, a thing which it is hard to imagine 'in areas where moisture is more abundant. Having fought these conditions for a number of years, as the report points out, over 90 per cent of these settlers moved out. They left the area, having lost in many cases their health, their ambition and whatever capital they may have had. Although a drive through that area to-day reveals a tragic picture, it is not as tragic as it would have been about ten years ago because then one would have seen many abandoned homesteads with windows boarded up, whereas to-day most of them have been torn down or taken away. The only evidence that at one time that land had been settled is furnished by the spectacle of rocks that have been cleared from the land and piled in rows, north and south and east and west, representing many long years of toil on the part of these farmers, who eventually had to move owing to the extreme drought.
I should like again to say how much the farmers who stayed in that area have been helped under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act gave them a kind of drought relief and made it possible for them to exist. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act made it possible for them to store up water for their stock in dug-outs. Unfortunately, in that area the run-off from snow is so uncertain that in many years these dug-outs dry up and the farmers are not able to use the pasture that the dug-out is supposed to water. The construction of the Red Deer diversion scheme would change the whole picture. The pastures would be provided with water on a permanent basis. To a great extent irrigation would provide insurance against crop failure, and the farmers would be able to increase the size of their herds knowing full well that they would have the TMr. Quelch.]
water to water them and the feed from the irrigated land to feed them in times of dry years.
The cost of getting the water from the Red Deer river to Hamilton lake would be $6,700,000. It would probably cost a similar amount to get the water from Hamilton lake on to the land. That work would be done by the provincial governments, the municipalities, and the federal government working together; but the cost of getting the water from the Red Deer to Hamilton lake should be borne by the federal government as a national undertaking because it is of direct benefit to the whole of the dominion of Canada. The financial cost of constructing this project would be small as compared with the losses incurred in the area since settlement. In the past, millions of dollars have been lost in that area, partly as a result of the heavy expenditures for drought relief, partly as a result of the loss of revenue due to crop failure and partly, of course, as a result of the loss of markets in so far as eastern Canada is concerned.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that moneys will be made available for a number of these projects from vote No. 606 of $10,000,000. He included the Red Deer scheme, but he made it clear that this money is not for the purpose of starting construction on the projects but rather for cost of engineers' work in checking these surveys. I hope that it will be possible for the federal government actually to start construction work on this and other projects in western Canada at the earliest possible date. I know it is felt that the government should not start projects of this kind until unemployment increases. On the other hand, if the work could be carried out now, by the time the slump arrives, which most people fear may come in two or three years from now-and of which they were warned by the governor of the Bank of Canada-and if those projects were completed we would hav^ available land for around thirty thousand people. These people would be on a self-sustaining basis. If, on the other hand, we wait until the slump comes along we can provide employment on this scheme for around 1,500 men. But if the job was completed we would have additional homesteads for around thirty thousand people. I do not think any time should be lost in starting to carry out the project at an early date.
This is just one example of the utilization of the waters from the watershed of the Saskatchewan river. I am strongly in favour, and this group strongly favours the conservation

speechtext:
At the commencement may I pay my tribute to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) for the interest that he has taken over the years in western development. He is one of those members of parliament who have contributed much to the welfare of this country. To-day, after several years of advocating the necessity of irrigation and power development in western Canada, many who previously scoffed at the necessity of such works being undertaken are giving support to the ideas that have been his for all those years.
In the constituency of Lake Centre the attitude of the large majority of the people is one of high commendation and appreciation for the work and activities of the hon. member for Davenport.
May I first of all deal with the motion itself? The motion provides for a request to the government to take into immediate consideration the advisability of introducing legislation to set up a permanent interprovincial board or commission on which the three prairie provinces and the dominion would have equal representation. In other words, this resolution requests the government to set up a board or commission under the chairmanship of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or some other qualified person, to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed, and particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river.
I am one of those who support this resolution because of the necessity of something being done as provided for in the resolution, but at the same time I maintain the stand I have taken at all times, that judges ought not to serve on royal commissions. I am sure that this resolution will receive the support of members on all sides of the house. In point of fact, if this resolution were carried into effect it would implement the recommendations of the advisory committee on reconstruction, which made its final report on September 24, 1943, the. report in question being one by a subcommittee on the conservation and development of natural resources. This subcommittee was set up to study the natural resources of Canada, particularly water and power, with a view to providing employment after the cessation of hostilities, and also for the purpose of recommending long-term policies necessary to safe-63260- 42i
guard these resources. The main resources which have to be safeguarded are the resources of water with a view to conserving moisture, developing power and assuring irrigation. I am going to refer to some portions of this report so that the minister in replying may be able to give to the house and to the country some information as to the extent to which the recommendations have been implemented.
On page 6 of the report the recommendation is made that:
An early decision should be reached as to the sharing of costs as between federal and provincial authorities in implementing the policies herein recommended, or such as may be adopted. This can only be done by conference between the authorities concerned. The longer-term programmes of conservation, of research, and of surveys may be considered to be properly the responsibility of the federal government.
I should like the minister to advise the house and the country to what extent this recommendation has been carried into effect, and in particular what decisions have been arrived at as to the sharing of costs as between federal and provincial authorities.
With reference to the resolution in question, I find the following recommendations with respect to water and power resources an page 15 of the report:
A.	The provision of immediate post-war employment.
B.	A long-term, or continuous policy, to assist to assist in the use and control of water on the basis of sound conservation.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the fact that over a long period of years western Canada, and in particular Saskatchewan and southern Alberta, has been subject to recurrent droughts. He mentioned the Palliser expedition. I had an opportunity of discussing that expedition on a number of occasions with John Moberley of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, who died some years ago at the age of almost one hundred years. He was the water boy and last survivor of the Palliser expedition. He particularly emphasized that during that expedition their greatest fear was not death from starvation but from lack of water. He told me that on one occasion Palliser had stated that this area never would be settled. That was also the view of the then leaders of the Roman Catholic church and in particular of the archbishop, Tache, who 'in 1867 after crossing this area expressed the belief that it would never be suitable for agriculture. The report to which I am referring deals with this situation. At page 16 it says:
Water Conservation

In the great plains region of western Canada, and in central British Columbia, many areas have insufficient precipitation for the successful pursuit of agriculture. Irrigation in these areas is necessary, and the conservation, control and distribution of both surface and underground water supplies is of vital importance. The use of the rivers of the great plains region in Canada raises both interprovincial and international problems.
After setting out the necessity for water storage and irrigation projects in the drought areas being proceeded with under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act it indicates what should be followed in the matter of a longterm policy:
The continuation and systematic extension of basic water resources investigations by the dominion water and power bureau in collaboration with the provinces . . .
Then on page 18 it recommends what the hon. member for Davenport has included in this resolution, namely the setting up of a permanent board or commission, This is the recommendation:
The setting up of a western provinces water board to include representatives of the dominion and the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba for the purpose of advising the respective governments on the most equitable and advantageous use of the limited water supplies in the great plains region of Canada.
Therefore, sir, I am sure that from all parts of this house will come support for this resolution in its present form. It asks for no expenditure of money at this time, but it does ask for immediate consideration of a problem that will be recurrent in the years to come, namely the problem of drought. It asks that necessary measures be taken to ensure that never again shall we in Saskatchewan and Alberta pass through the conditions so ably and vividly described this afternoon by the hon. fnember for Rosetown-Biggar, conditions which could have been avoided if parliaments, realizing that recurrent droughts do take place in western Canada, had carried out a system of public works of irrigation to the end that, instead of the devastation that prevailed between 1930 and 1939, there would have been a degree of production which would have done away with the necessity of providing money for direct and indirect relief in those provinces.
I realize that something has been done; but too little has been done. This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) referred to the fact that some portion of the $10,000,000 which is to be voted may be used for this purpose; in other words, that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration may use some portion of this vote to carry out survey and engineering works. These
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)
works are to be undertaken for three purposes; first, to secure and assure employment; second, in the larger field, to protect western Canada from' the effects of recurrent droughts, and, finally,, to assure the development of power and irrigation projects. I am particularly interested in what has been done because of the fact that, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in the centre of my constituency is the largest lake in central Saskatchewan. It was a navigable lake which was utilized for the transportation of wheat from central, eastern and middle western Saskatchewan down its entire length and ultimately on to the C.P.R. main line, thence to the markets of eastern Canada. Today that lake is in grave danger of drying up. Between April, 1944, and October, 1945, its depth decreased by two feet. Its shore areas are becoming infested with weeds. This lake is worth preserving as a reservoir for conserving and distributing moisture, through irrigation, along the Qu'Appelle valley. It is worth preserving for the production of fish. It is worth preserving as the finest sanctuary for wild -bird life to be found anywhere in central Saskatchewan. Finally, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggests, it is worth preserving as a .playground, having on its shores some of the largest resorts in Saskatchewan.

pointed out that as far as this lake was concerned there was no place in Saskatchewan where the expenditure of money would pay greater dividends in enjoyment, in the preservation of an agricultural area, in the conservation of bird life and the development of irrigation by the diversion of the surplus waters of the South Saskatchewan river.
There are those who say that to-day is not the time for public works or expenditures. There are others who say that we should wait a little longer. I brought these matters up last November when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) were before the committee, and he quite frankly stated that the matter was not within his jurisdiction, but that it came within that of the Minister of Agriculture, being a matter which could be dealt with under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
I do not want to see the expenditure of large sums of money for public works unless the works undertaken are to be reasonably self-liquidating. I have before me two alternative plans for irrigation in Saskatchewan. According to the consulting engineer under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, both these plans, one involving the expenditure of $28 million and the other of $39 million, would be self-liquidating. One must keep this fact in mind, aside altogether from the further fact that these developments would serve areas which year by year would yield crops where, in the past, from year to year during the draught periods the same areas yielded nothing but drought, grasshoppers and all manner of difficulties. And, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has pointed out, the debt piled up from year to year.
These projects are necessary in the interests of the survival of Saskatchewan. They will ensure employment to-day. I am not one who from time to time comes before the government and, while preaching the necessity for retrenchment, at the same time asks for large expenditures which would not be self-liquidating or beneficial. I believe a reduction in taxation must come immediately if industry in this country is to provide the jobs so necessary for our returning men, and for those who have been discharged in recent months from munitions factories and other war industry in general.
I was much disturbed the other day upon reading the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in this connection. He placed before the country a most dangerous doctrine in a speech he delivered in answer to a conference which met here, namely, the delegation from the Canadian and Catholic Federation of Labour, protesting against the
loan being made to Great Britain. He stated that it had taken him a whole month to understand the necessity for this loan. Then, as reported in the press, he said:
If the loan w'as not granted the Canadian government might be forced into the position of having to cut off family allowance payments, which now total between $200 million and $250 million annually, and it might also have to default in the payment of interest on victory bonds.
If those statements were made-and they have not been denied by the minister-they represent the expression of a dangerous viewpoint at a time like this.
I am not one who wants to add to the clamour for works which will not be self-liquidating. But if that statement be true, and if the minister meant what he said, then the financial position of this country is very serious. Those who are answerable for it are the members of the government who, in recent years, have gone out of their way to secure the support of the country by making promises for expenditures far beyond those which should have been made, having regard to present conditions. I am not referring to war expenditures, either, not in any sense of the word.
Is it not strange that one minister says we are in a terrible condition, when only the other day the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) said at a banquet in his honour that conditions were so fine in Canada he expected income taxation would be cut by 50 per cent at this session?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the resolution which has been proposed by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), may I congratulate him not only on having brought forward this important motion but on the excellent work he has done in this direction over a long period of years. The resolution reads:
That. in. the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of introducing legislation during this session to set up a permanent interprovincial board or commisison on which the three p'rairie provinces and the dominion would have equal representation under the chairmanship of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or some other qualified person, to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watfrshed of the Saskatchewan river.

Water Conservation
I am sure that hon. members in all parts of the house will agree with the principle of the resolution, which asks that a careful investigation be made into this subject. As was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the reconstruction committee gave long study to the whole question during the session of 1943. At that time they considered the matter in connection with the problems of reconstruction and made a recommendation in the report which they submitted following their investigation. I would join with the hon. member in requesting the minister, when he replies, to tell us what has been done with respect to that recommendation and whether any arrangements have been negotiated between the federal authorities on the one hand, and, on the other, the various provinces concerned.
I was born and brought up within the Palliser triangle and I have farmed there for the past twenty-five years. I also had the privilege of serving on the advisory committee under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act for a number of years before coming to this house, and I have witnessed great changes in scientific agriculture, in methods of tillage and cultivation, in soil conservation and the development of rust-resisting cereals, improvement in the production of live stock, and man}- other similar questions; but certainly [DOT] the most important of all these matters has been water development and conservation.
You cannot produce foodstuffs of any kind in this country without water; water is the most essential element in any production of foodstuffs. The reclamation possibilities, under proper development and conservation of water, are immense, a fact which has been pretty well proven by the efforts that have been made under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Those ' who have been administering that legislation since its inception in 1935 can substantiate this.
Possibly there has not been accomplished under the board quite as much as many of us would have liked to see, but one thing that has been achieved is this:	They have established what can be done as a result of the conservation of water. As was pointed out this afternoon, when we realize what quantities of water are wasted every spring from the various streams and rivers, we realize how much can be accomplished by the proper control of these streams for the promotion of agricultural production throughout the year.
May I refer to a pamphlet entitled, "P.F.R.A. and their Record of Achievement", which was issued in 1943. From 1935 to 1943 a great deal was accomplished; but since then, owing to
the war effort, the achievements have been more or less nullified. At page 55 of the pamphlet reference is made to the work accomplished under P.F.R.A. From the inauguration of the programme in 1935 to March 31, 1943, the water development work that has been accomplished has included the maintenance of water supply to take care of 50,000 acres of irrigated land and existing projects; repairs have been carried out, and so on. It lists the number carried out, and states that the amount spent up to that date for water development and 'conservation alone was $2,124,722. Much more than that was spent in connection with community pastures, reforestation, regrassing and other matters of that kind.
This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) telling about the difficulties which the people of the three prairie provinces passed through in the early thirties. I experienced all the conditions as he portrayed them. Southern Saskatchewan suffered more severely than any other part of those provinces as a result of the drought at that time. One could drive for days and not see any vegetation whatever. There was no water to be seen anywhere, and one marvelled how the women and children on those farms existed at all during that period. The corner I lived in, in southwestern Manitoba, was on the fringe of that area.
When we remember what those people had produced in years prior to that period and contrast it with their privations during those years, I do not think anyone would object to a survey, and even to a considerable expenditure of money, for the purpose of finding out what can be made possible through proper water conservation, so as to conserve the runoff from the large rivers coming from the mountains. Someone mentioned a lake this afternoon. I remember driving along lake Johnstone, south of Moose Jaw, during those dry years. Tire lake was perfectly dry, not a drop of water being at the bottom.
On all hands people boast of our great agricultural production during the war years, and I do not think it would have been possible had it not been for what had been accomplished in the prairie provinces under P.F.R.A. Development and conservation made it possible for many people to maintain live stock, to produce dairy products, to cultivate fine vegetable gardens for themselves where previously in average years they had been unable to do anything of the sort.
It is difficult to estimate in dollars and cents how much extra we were able to produce for the war effort, as far as foodstuffs are concerned, as a result of the work done by that board throughout the prairies. I remem-
Water Conservation

ber reading in the fall of 1943, in a magazine called Canadian Business, an article pointing out the trend that had been observed in western Canada. The writer of that article stated that in the early twenties seventy per cent of the farmers' income was from wheat and cereal products and that position had been reversed so that less than forty per cent of their income was now obtained from that source.
I maintain that the greatest part of the change-over was made possible by the efforts of those operating under P.F.R.A. in large areas of those three provinces in connection with the development of water, regrassing, and community pastures. We were simply experimenting and the expenditure was not large-a very few million dollars, as had been pointed out. If such results could be obtained there, I am sure that our potentialities along those lines are still considerable.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated this afternoon that, apart from the vote this year of $3,000,000, an amount of $10,000000 was to be made available through the Department of Reconstruction for survey work along these lines. The other day I read an article, under the date of April 5, by Doctor Archibald, director of experimental farms in Canada. He, along with the deputy minister of agriculture, Doctor Barton, had more to do with directing the efforts of the prairie farm rehabilitation work in the prairie provinces than anybody else. In his address at Guelph the other day he referred to the fact that $110 million were to be spent on some project in the prairie provinces in the near future. I am not sure what it is. That is quite a large sum of money the department is to spend.
I support this resolution wholeheartedly. While we have accomplished this fine piece of work in the prairie provinces, it is practically nothing when compared with what our neighbours to the south have done. This afternoon the hon. member for Davenport, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and others told of the magnificent achievements with respect to water conservation and irrigation in certain parts of the United States. That has been done. In to-day's Christian Science Monitor, a Boston paper, I noticed a full page devoted to this type of work. The heading is "Flood wall at Kansas City paces vast drive to tame Missouri river." It goes on to point out that the sum of $7 billion has been set aside for this work, and that $1,500 million is to be spent on the Missouri river. It will affect some ten states and bring about irrigation and improvement of agricultural productivity in the states concerned. If they can

' do that in the United States surely it should be an example to this country as to what we must do in the interests of our own people, and more especially in the interests of world food production.
Throughout history the majority of the people of the world have been undernourished. To-day we hear much of world government and international agreements. If this is to become a fact, then we in this country have great possibilities and responsibilities to produce much more food than we have ever done in the past. Therefore I think this resolution is most timely and we would be neglecting our duty if all quarters of the house did not support it. We should see that a thorough investigation is carried out. Like the hon. members who spoke this afternoon, I believe that at this time all large expenditures of public money should be self-liquidating. It is a matter of surveying. I am satisfied that it ivould be self-liquidating. A few million dollars is a lot of money, but in comparison with government expenditures to-day very little has been spent on P.F.R.A. It has returned many times the amount to the citizens of western Canada and to this nation as a whole. I am pleased to have the opportunity of endorsing this resolution which, I am sure, will be accepted in all corners of the house.

Just
to prove that there is nothing political in this matter, I rise as a representative of our party in Alberta to support my old friend who knows every rock in the Mackenzie river and every blade of grass grown out there. I hold in my hand a clipping from the East Central Irrigation Association which quotes Herbert Hoover, one-time president of the United States, as saying that every drop of water that runs to the sea without rendering a commercial return is a public waste. Perhaps we can all agree that Mr. Hoover has at last said something that is really worth while.
We shall be told something about the expenditure of money, and I have no doubt of the position of those of us who criticize the government for overexpenditures and then in the next breath urge them to spend something more. I appreciate that position to the fullest, but I may be permitted to criticize and to doubt the wisdom of the way in which they spend other people's money. It has got abroad in this country, through the various information agencies which rude people occasionally suggest are propaganda agencies, that there is a feeling that they may be tainted just a little bit with the government's idea and that they might assist them in remaining where they are.

Water Conservation
I, of course, know nothing about that. I am quite sure the ministers would not consciously do that, but perhaps some of the chaps who work for them know where their bread is buttered and occasionally they may slip into political propaganda. That is gentle criticism.
On the large question of sectionalism which has so often been raised, I wish to say that in a portion of western Canada we are seeking to have this government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, undertake a large project. Therefore I immediately say to my hon. friends who come from Ontario and Quebec that what we are seeking is a few canals. We want these canals to carry water in order that we may raise food. You have your canals here to carry bottoms. Ontario did not pay for them. Quebec is not going to pay for the St. Lawrence waterways. The point I am anxious to make, whether I succeed or not, is that because of the geographic location of an enterprise it cannot just immediately be said that it was done to help one province or two provinces or one area. In my judgment, what my old and hon. friend-and when I say "old" I mean I have known him a long time-* the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) said was well put. If improvements were brought about out in that country this would spread. Take the little Lethbridge Northern. I see the hon. gentleman writing at his desk who knows much more about it than I do. But what has happened there? They have a wonderful show going; they have sugar refineries and, in the last few years a canning factory. I do not care where hon. members live, they cannot buy canned vegetables that will even compare with those that are canned right now in Lethbridge. All that is the result of irrigating some land and making it productive.
I do not know how many hon. members have visited the town of Brooks. I am quite sure many of us do not even know that it exists. I give the house my word for this, there are no finer homes, there are no more healthy or contented people throughout Canada than those who live in that irrigated area. What strikes one so forcibly is this. You go about three miles south of Brooks, turn right and then you strike the main canal which comes from the dam at Bassano. There you have on one side of the road gardens blooming like the rose. Another fifteen miles away you come to the area of Scandia and Rainier, a small area. There is not enough grass growing there on fifty, acres to support a sheep, let alone a cow or steer that someone mentioned a moment ago.
What are these lands that we are seeking to do something with? Take an area out there where we have some land that is most unusual. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) is not in his seat at the moment; perhaps he knew I was going to say all these things; but it got so dry out there at one time some years ago that after the farmers had sold their fence posts in order to get the last dollar they could, the city council of Medicine Hat got a rainmaker by the name of Hatfield. He built a thing that looked like an oil derrick, although it was not so high. Up there he lit a fire and brewed some kind of witch's stew; I do not know what it was. He was paid on the basis of an inch and a half of rain or nothing. He lit this pot-I think he was just cooking himself a cup of coffee or something of the kind- but in any event they had a wonderful rain. Those hon. members who read Time magazine will know that Hatfield is still going. Down in San Diego a short time ago, when they had that young world's fair and the country was dry, they hired him and he guaranteed two inches of rain. They got seven inches and everybody in San Diego was flooded out. Then they had to pay him again to get it to stop. Of course he had nothing to do with it, but I tell that story for this reason. When people are driven to such straits that they will hire a charmer to try to induce a little bit of rain, conditions are serious. I have lived in that section of the country for a long time, and am familiar with the constituency of Acadia, from whose hon. member we heard this afternoon. I used to go there to shoot partridge.

But matters got so bad there that even the weeds would not grow and there were no partridge; that is why I stopped going to the hon. member's constituency. I was there quite often, however, and I did see this more than once. I would see a man and his wife and kids driving out behind a team, the harness held together with hay wire. If they were lucky, in the back end of the wagon they had a cow tied. They used a hay-rack because they could put on it all their kitchen stuff and bits of furniture; and they were going to some other place. Why? Because of lack of moisture.
I am anxious that one scheme be undertaken, and we have heard that a beginning is to be made in connection with the Red Deer

river development. I do not think the hon. member for Davenport occupied all the time of the engineers when he was in western Canada recently; perhaps it would be better to say that they occupied all his time, but in any event these same men tell me that from that development, which includes a 150-foot dam, we can get enough power to electrify all the farms in that part of the country. Let us be practical; let us see where our money is going. We gave out relief in large sums in that area, and as someone has so well said we got nothing from it except a number of angry people. I am quite sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr, Gardiner) would appreciate that if he were here, because he gave them all this dough; then everybody voted against him and threw out his outfit, so that it is difficult to buy votes in that way. I like the direct method; $2, and nobody says anything about it.
In any event, we have spent all this money and we have received nothing from it. With respect, sir, I say that in that arid land when they have rain they raise wonderful crops. I have seen them grow sixty bushels of wheat to the acre around Medicine Hat, and I am not using a bit of imagination. The land is tremendously fertile if only it can get some moisture. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) put it, it needs just that other inch. I think he is wrong; I have a record of the moisture every year from 1933 to 1946. And I believe we need more than another inch; certainly that is so in a bad year.
What happens when you get an irrigation system out there? Practically no wheat is grown at Brooks to-day. It becomes a specialized business; seed crops, peas, beans, small fruits and that sort of thing. I mean it is not going to increase the thing of which we have most, and I agree that there should be no difficulty about that. It becomes a specialized show. We will not interfere with your markets here, because we cannot ship these products that far. No matter how good we are, we just cannot overcome the north shore of lake Superior. I see the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is here; probably he is going to tell me more about coal before this session is finished, but he knows there are transportation difficulties. In all seriousness, I say that we in this house should regard this as a national problem, as it is. The Ontario canals were national problems. All we want is canals. We will use them for a different purpose; but will anyone tell me that we in the west got any benefit from the canals in eastern Canada? Of course we did not, but we did not complain;

we figured it was in the interests of the country that this should 'be done. So that all we are asking is a few canals which will generally add to the wealth of Canada, as I am quite sure the little bits of ditches here in the east have done.
Now a word as to money. I do not know anything about money; that is, about cost, and in that respect I like the terms of the resolution, which asks that a complete examination of the picture should be made.
I cannot sit down without giving the house a history of irrigation in our province. The Canadian Pacific railway had both the eastern irrigation scheme and the western scheme, coming from the Bow river. They spent millions of dollars and then gave it all away; houses, horses, machinery, ditches-one conduit over two miles long, just east of the town of Brooks-land and everything else including $450,000 as working capital. They gave it all away in order to get out of it. Why? Their irrigation fee was 50 cents an acre. They have some good men in that district. They took hold of the thing, raised the fee to $1 an acre, and then got tough. As everyone knows, nobody will pay the government or the Canadian Pacific railway anything if they can possibly avoid doing so. That just seems to be true throughout the length and breadth of this country; and nobody paid the C.P.R. So that they found themselves supporting this thing with tremendous losses every year. I believe the district took it over about five or six years ago. Their ditches are clean; their roads are good, and instead of working capital of $450,000 to-day they have working capital of well over $1,000,000. That shows what can be done if the people who are there take an interest in the picture.
At the session before last of the Alberta legislature a similar group took over the western district, which is immediately east of Calgary, in around Strathmore and Gleichen. The C.P.R. gave them the same amount of money. They could not give them the land, because they did not own it any longer, but even in one short year they are making a success of that business. The Lethbridge Northern, as hon. members know, is a government-supported affair, and it seems to me that when we have operation by governments or railroads we get into trouble. But if we can have local management of these things they can be made successful and, as my hon. friend has told us, they can become self-liquidating propositions. Why, in the eastern irrigation district they grow fruit; they grow anything there.
