Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this resolution I wish first to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) to whom all westerners owe a great deal. All of us appreciate his efforts to educate the public of Canada to the very great need for irrigation In western Canada.
I particularly wish to thank the hon. member for the map indicating the Saskatchewan river power, navigation and irrigation rehabilitation scheme which he has proposed.
A large part of the constituency of Wey-burn, which I have the good fortune to represent, is embraced in this project, for it includes the Soo line district, as well as the Regina plains and Areola line areas. In this region are located the Souris river, Long and Was-cana creeks; and may I say that this is one of the most productive areas in the whole of Saskatchewan.
Most western people are interested in irrigation, for the greatest natural hazards in the southern portions of Saskatchewan and Alberta are the fairly frequent and all too regular cycles of drought. According to records, droughts occurred during the periods 1838-48, 1885-95 and 1929-3S. It appears that drought is widespread in the prairie provinces every thirty years or so and extends over a decade with a varying degree of intensity. The worst year which the western agriculturist has experienced was 1937. That year
half the population of Saskatchewan was forced to accept government relief and the whole situation savoured of a national calamity. On that occasion the federal authorities came to the aid of provincial governments in the west, and kind-hearted folk from all parts of Canada dispatched trainloads of food and clothing to aid the stricken people of the plains.
On that occasion live stock were slaughtered by the thousands because of lack of water and the scarcity of fodder with which to feed them.
Fine herds of cattle were marketed for $8 and 810 a head. Other thousands were transported east and west of the prairies where fodder was available. Trainloads of grain and other fodder were shipped to the west at great expense to the public to keep alive the relatively few remaining animals the people were permitted to retain on the farm. I believe this catastrophe could have been averted had a programme of water conservation been embarked upon years ago. A programme embracing the construction of small dams, dug-outs, and small irrigation projects would have provided water for live stock and the much needed fodder for their sustenance.
Such a scheme, together with larger irrigation projects as envisaged by the resolution before the house, while incurring the initial outlay of considerable sums of money would lend stability to western agriculture and create a prosperous farming population, so necessary to the prosperity of the whole national economy.
Everyone agrees that irrigation on a large scale requires detailed planning in engineering and an exhaustive study of the economic aspects involved. I believe, if this is done, that irrigation of the western prairies will be found to be economically sound and a profitable investment.
Anyone who has inspected the 500,000 acres of irrigated land in Alberta will recognize the great material advantages accruing from such development.
Irrigated land supports from nine to ten times as many people there as do the dry farming areas surrounding those projects.
There are 4.600 prosperous farmers in the district, making for a steadying influence on Alberta's economy. Over a ten-year period the average wheat production exceeded dry area yield by almost twelve bushels an acre. If we assume that this whole irrigated area produced nothing but wheat that would mean almost S7 million worth' of new wealth for Alberta every year. But other crops are produced in this region, all of which produce more per acre than wheat. For instance,
Water Conservation

eleven per cent of the sugar production of Canada comes from sugar beets produced in this area.
Irrigation is necessary for the economic stabilization of the western provinces. In order to achieve a well-balanced and stable economy there must be diversification of industry.
The whole matter of irrigation must be approached from the national viewpoint, since Canadian prosperity and well-being are impossible while a large area of the prairies is subject to the wide fluctuations of income caused by repeated crop failures induced by drought. A stabilized western economy would create a steady market for eastern manufactured commodities. The establishment of secondary industries for the processing of primary products from the farm would create more wealth in the west and for Canada. They would employ many workers who must of necessity consume primary products and the goods from Canadian factories. Without irrigation and its attendant hydro development many such industries could not be established.
In closing, may I enumerate some of the major benefits that would result from western irrigation:
(1) It would permit a greater range of diversified crop production and an increase in live stock population.	,
(2)	It would tend to stabilize crop production and would ensure against total crop failure.
(3)	Stability of farm tenure would be established with a higher standard of living.
(4) A broad, sound base for industrial development would be set up.
(5)	Electric power for industry and rural electrification would be created.
(6)	There would be established a source of stable revenue for the municipal, provincial and federal governments of the country.
I shall support the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house moved by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of introducing legislation during this session to set up a permanent interprovincial board or commission on which the three prairie provinces and the dominion would have equal representation under the chairmanship of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or some other qualified person, to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of .the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river.
[Mr. McKay.)
The contents of this resolution have been discussed many times in this house, always under the auspices of the bon. gentleman. He has now, I think, gained for the proposal he has announced in this house during many years support which I am sure must be gratifying to him, and I congratulate him upon the method and determination with which he has continued his fight for water for the prairie provinces, although, being an eastern member, he is not so politically identified with those particular provinces. I like to think of him as a. very close friend, not as a member of a constituency but as a citizen of Canada, knowing that in what he now .proposes in his motion that is now before the house he is dealing with a matter that will have an effect upon the economic life of all Canada and not upon any particular constituency.
In this proposal he is asking for the setting u.p of a commission, and I should like to deal with the history of the transactions that have taken place since the natural resources were transferred to the province of Alberta in 1930. I was asked a question in the house by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) and also by another hon. member as to what the government had done in the light of the reports that had come from the committee. The hon. member for Davenport divided his motion into two parts.
In the first instance, he spoke of the conservation of water and dealt more particularly with conditions in Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) also followed the same line as far as Alberta was concerned. In the second place, the hon. member for Davenport dealt with it from the point of view of the watershed on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. There are two different proposals, both related to each other .but both similar, although easily distinguished.
With regard to the first of these, I may say that the rivers of the prairie provinces are interprovincial or international in character. Every important stream in those provinces is shared by another province, by the northwest territories or by the states that are immediately over the border. From the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains the main sources of water flow easterly across the three provinces and northerly to the northwest territories, and the boundaries of those political divisions bear no relation to the physical characteristics of the areas which they include.
Prior to 1930 all these waters were administered by the dominion, -which greatly simplified all questions of use and control. From the first settlements on the prairie up to that

Water Conservation
date a large number of water rights were granted by the Department of the Interior with an almost complete absence of litigation between interests claiming conflicting rights, and no questions arose as between one province and another. Since the transfer of the natural resources, four jurisdictions-the dominion and the three provinces-administer these same waters. While up to the present no serious difficulties have arisen, minor questions having been settled in an amicable manner, it does not follow that the need for planning and apportionment has lessened by the lapse of time. The contrary is true.
Following the transfer of the natural resources there came a long period of depression when there was no incentive for new undertakings. This was partly overcome by the activities of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration. It is interesting and, I am sure, gratifying to all members of the house to hear the praise that has been lavished upon the work of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration. I am sure that will encourage them to carry on even in a larger degree than they have done hitherto.
Changed conditions are favourable for new developments, many of which have been planned and some have already been authorised. Never before have the use and conservation of the prairie water supply been so needed. I doubt if there are two things more needed in the Dominion of Canada than, first, water, and then, oil. This department has been endeavouring as best it can with all the facilities and resources at its command to find both.
This department is satisfied that a board or authority of some kind is necessary to assist and advise in the administration of all interprovincial waters and that the dominion is entitled to representation on such a board as the administrator of the northwest territories. as being responsible for international boundary w'aters and by reason of its operations under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
Action to set up a board representative of the three prairie provinces and the dominion which would examine and report upon the most effective use or control of waters common to two or more of the parties was begun as soon as the agreement for the transfer from the dominion to the provinces of resources, including water resources, was completed in 1930. It was intended that this agreement, which was drawn and which was submitted to' the provinces, should become effective about the same time as the transfer agreements. For this purpose negotiations were entered into with the provincial premiers and a draft
agreement to establish a western provinces water board was prepared by this department. That was accepted by the provinces and signed by the three premiers under date of the 24th October, 1930. For some reason there were some clauses in it which seemed to operate unfairly against the dominion, and Justice, at that time being consulted, were not in favour of the agreement as drawn.
It was not until 1937 that the province of Manitoba began to make inquiries with regard to the rehabilitation plans for the western drought areas which called for taking water from interprovincial streams, such as the South Saskatchewan river, and which it was feared might affect future power developments within the province. Consideration was sought for the establishment of such a board to anticipate the problems which might arise and thereby avoid possible disputes relating to interprovincial streams.
The then minister, the Hon. Mr. Crerar, replied on April 16, 1937, that he was in favour of such a board; and that it would prove of very great value for the purpose intended. He said that he was in favour of carrying on the negotiations with respect to the formation of the board and that he would be glad to communicate with the other provinces in due course. A few days later he wrote to the ministers in charge of water resources in Alberta and Saskatchewan suggesting that the agreement of 1930 be brought up to date- I am speaking of 1937 now-and the objectives of the board and the proposed method of operations be discussed between the responsible technical officers.
Hon. Mr. Kerr, the natural resources minister of Saskatchewan, immediately replied as favouring the board and referred to the recent amendment to the water rights act, 1931, which authorized him as minister to enter into agreements with the other provinces and the dominion for the establishment of a board to control the use of interprovincial waters. The other ministers stated that they were prepared to give the proposal careful consideration.
A new agreement was drawn, prepared by this department and submitted to the three provincial ministers concerned. The new draft proposed an arrangement much simpler than the previous one. Instead of an agreement between governments, it was to be an agreement hetween the ministers responsible for the administration of water resources in the four areas, and was to be advisory only. I have the substance of the agreement here, but I do not think I need trouble the house with the terms of it except to say that the

Water Conservation
rights of the dominion were protected. The powers of the advisory board were set out clearly and in detail.
The basic principle underlying the formation of the board wTas that it would be a technical board consisting of the officers responsible for the detailed administration of water resources in each of the jurisdictions affected and reporting t-o the ministers in executive control of these resources.
The new draft was accepted by Mr. Kerr for Saskatchewan on June 30, 1937, and by Mr. McDiarmid for Manitoba on October 8 of the same year, but the Alberta minister declined to take action, although pressed to do so by the Alberta director of water resources.
The matter was again brought to the attention of the Alberta minister, now the Hon. Mr. MacMillan, by the acting deputy minister of this department on August 11, 1941. Mr. MacMillan replied on January 2, 1942, to the effect that his province did not see the need of such a board on the grounds that Saskatchewan was the only province that could be affected by rights granted by Alberta and that so far the authorities in Saskatchewan had not intimated that they wished to discuss any questions. There was a further exchange of letters shortly after, but Mr. MacMillan remained unconvinced.
There was no further action at that time, but the approaching end of the war brought a renewed interest throughout the west in large-scale projects for irrigation and power. During 1944, boards of trade at Saskatoon, Prince Albert and Perdue in Saskatchewan, and Drum-heller and Craigmile in Alberta passed resolutions asking the Department of Mines and Resources to set up a water board for the prairie provinces:	[DOT]
. . . whose duty it would be, among others, to assemble all the available stream flow data of western rivers and establish such new stations as may be required to get a complete record of the river discharge throughout the whole western drainage area, and to determine the most feasible and economical water power and irrigation projects that would make the best use of all the available drainage water, with the object of advising the various governments concerned of the possibilities of the area.
The establishment of such a board has also seen endorsed by the dominion subcommittee on agriculture and combined resources set up in connection with the reconstruction programme of the dominion-provincial conference.
In consequence of these large-scale irrigation and other projects proposed as a post-war measure of rehabilitation, the department again wrote to Mr. MacMillan on June 13, 1944, suggesting that if, in view of this changed situation, Mr. MacMillan was agreeable to

having a board constituted under section 64 of the Alberta Water Resources Act, which provides appropriate authority, the minister would be glad to review the matter with the responsible ministers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba who had previously expressed their approval.
There is no reply to- this letter on file, and so far as the dominion is concerned the matter rests at this stage.
Within a few months after the minister's last letter to Mr. MacMillan, the provinces took action without reference to the dominion. At a meeting held at Saskatoon on September 21, 1944, it was decided by Hon. N. E. Tanner, Alberta minister of lands and mines, Hon.
J.	H. Phelps, Saskatchewan minister of natural resources, and Hon. J. S. McDiarmid, Manitoba minister of mines and) natural resources, to establish a water board representative of the three prairie provinces under an agreement along the lines of that prepared by this department in 1937.
At the time of this meeting it was the understanding of those present that the board should be advisory only and should have no jurisdiction in the matter of allocating water rights with respect to' interprovincial watersheds as between the three provinces concerned.
Some time elapsed before the formal agreement was completed, this being dated December 7, 1945. The present representatives on the board are, for Alberta, Mr. Ben Russell, director of water resources; for Saskatchewan, Mr. G. N. Munro, chief engineer, water rights branch; and for Manitoba, Mr. D. M. Stephens, deputy minister of mines and natural resources.
Arrangements have been made for an organization meeting of the board to be held at Saskatoon on April 1 and 2. Questions relating to procedure as well as with regard to specific problems to which the board might devote immediate attention will probably be decided upon at that time.
It is understood that when the decision was made to set up the board the dominion was not asked to participate on account of objection by the representative of Alberta, but those from the other two provinces felt that, while it would be desirable to have the dominion interest in water resources represented, there would be a considerable advantage in having the work begun on a provincial basis.	,
That is the position so far as the conservation of water in Saskatchewan is concerned. An advisory board has been formed representing the three provinces, with no representation of the dominion upon it, and for that

Water Conservation
reason, as I said before, that is where the dominion goes out of the picture as at this stage.
The motion that is before the house aks for the setting up of an interprovincial board. I suggest that we as a dominion cannot set up through this house a board which is going to take over the jurisidiction of either of the three provinces and that any board that is set up must be with the consent and approval of the three provinces. For that reason I suggest that that part of the hon. member's motion has already been met by the three provinces, which have made their choice of an advisory board.

I have already said that. I have also stated that when the agreement was being prepared by the dominion with the provinces the commission was to be of an advisory character, without any executive power.
The hon. member then addressed himself to the question of the protection of the forests on the east slope of the Rocky mountains. Here again I must give a little of the history of the forestry of the eastern slope.
The Rocky mountains forest reserve was established in 1911, at which time the dominion government through the dominion forest service of the Department of the Interior inaugurated a development policy of administration and protection, which continued until the transfer of the resources late in 1930. Complete control of all the natural resources within the boundaries of the forest reserve was vested in the forest service. These included fire protection, timber disposal, grazing uses, rental of surface rights, and mining claims, permits to hunters and trappers for the erection of cabins and many other miscellaneous uses.
While administration of hunting and fishing was a function of the province, a measure of control was exercised by the dominion forest officers through the requirement for travel permits; in fact, during periods of high fire hazards large sections of this area were closed to hunting and travel.
The total area of the east slope reserves as of 1930 was 13,786 square miles, but certain proposed additional areas were under consideration. When the province of Alberta took over these areas were added and the total area of provincial forest reserves on the east slope now stands at 14,266 square miles.
That land was divided into five units under the dominion. When the province took it over they made it into three and then began their jurisdiction to protect these forests. Unfortunately, the experience of the province was that the losses were much greater than they had been under the dominion government, the reason being that they had not the money necessary to provide that forest protection at that time.
Communications were exchanged between the province and the dominion with regard to the taking over of the east slope of the Rockies by the dominion, and in the first instance a letter was written on December 10, 1937, by the then provincial minister, Mr. N. E. Tanner, of which I have here a copy, dealing with the whole matter:
When in Ottawa recently my colleague-the Hon. Solon Low, provincial treasurer-had intended to discuss with you the matter of our
Water Conservation

forest reserves situate on the east slope of the Rocky mountains, but owing to your absence, also that of Doctor Camsell, he mentioned the subject to the department and I am writing at some length so that you may more fully understand our attitude.
As you are aware these reserves are considerably important when consideration is being given to the rehabilitation of the drought areas, as all our large rivers, with the exception of the Peace, have their source in the forest reserves.
While these waters are of importance to Alberta, they flow through our neighbouring province of Saskatchewan into Manitoba, and we feel that Alberta is entitled to some consideration in maintaining the organization established during the administration of the resources by the Department of the Interior. Such assistance might conceivably be along the lines of the Clarke-McXary legislation in the United States of America, with which no doubt your department is very well acquainted.
I understand that in the year 1924 the President of the United States of America gave his approval to "an act to provide for forest lands, for the reforestation of denuded areas, for the extension of national forests, and for other purposes in order to promote the continuous production of timber on lands chiefly suitable therefor," and in so doing the President and congress established on a statutory basis a fundamental forest policy for the United States . . .
You will readily appreciate that if the province were to discontinue this service we might anticipate a serious depletion of the forest cover within a few years, and the passing of this protection would have a considerable effect on the distribution of water throughout the following years.
So long as the east slope of the Rocky mountains is well timbered the periodic run-off will be well controlled by nature, but with the loss of the timber we could expect periods of high water in the early spring and the water courses practically, if not, dry, in the summer and fall seasons.
The importance of the east slope watershed has been recognized in publications that have been issued by various governmental departments, as the agricultural development depends for its success, to a large extent, on a dependable water supply for domestic use, power and especially. for irrigation projects.
Your department will have given these matters their earnest consideration in dealing with the rehabilitation programme for the drought areas, and the information as to stream measurements is a matter of record in your department: this work having been continued as a federal service under an arrangement with the province.

It is understood that the preliminary drafts of the agreement finally made in December. 1929. had continued this reservation, but for some unknown reason, this section was withdrawn from the agreement as completed.

Dear Mr. Crerar:
Re: protection of forests on the east slope of the Rocky mountains
Following our discussion in Ottawa on the 6th instant. I agreed to write you setting out as clearly as possible what I thought our programme should be regarding the above question. In doing this I shall set it out under separate points:
1.	The department of lands and mines and the Alberta government recognize the need of assisting forest fire prevention on all forested areas in the province, built to the most modern and efficient standard.
2.	As the east slope lies within the province of Alberta no other province is so intimately involved with the regulatory functions of forests in respect to water conservation. The stability of irrigation farming, of the beet sugar and canning industry, and of ranching, as well as water supplies for rural and urban settlement, is founded upon the constancy of stream flow and water level, largely dependent upon the condition of the watershed forest. The future of the forest industries is also dependent upon the continuance of forest growth.
3.	Alberta does not favour divided jurisdiction in the handling of any of the natural resources. The province opposes the administration of any portion of her forest domain by a forest service conducting its operations from the federal seat of government. Any such form of control is in our view dilatory in method and not always efficient.
4.	While opposed to the transfer of any portion of Alberta's forest area to dominion management. we feel that inasmuch as such watersheds affect the welfare of important areas beyond the provincial boundaries, it is the dominion government's responsibility to assist financially in the protection and management of the east slope watersheds.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will proceed with what I was going to say.
I should like to outline the general situation with respect to my own constituency

Water Conservation

as it bears on the subject-matter of this resolution as it was interpreted by the hon. member for Davenport. There are in southern Alberta wide areas of land which are rich and easy to work, and relatively near to railways and schools. This land .has nearly all been settled and brought under cultivation. The rainfall in this area is usually too scanty, and crop failures are therefore common. The climate is well adapted to growing sugar beets, canning crops, peas, beans, corn, tomatoes and all kinds of vegetables. It is also well adapted to the production of alfalfa and other hay crops and all kinds of grain. It is one of the greatest potential food-producing areas in this dominion. All that it requires is more water.
There are in my constituency four major irrigation projects. They are the Lethbridge-Colddale district, the Raymond irrigation district, the Magrath irrigation district and -the Taber irrigation district, comprising altogether 120,000 acres. These projects $re irrigated from the St. Mary's river through a canal built early in the century, from 1899 to 1901. Most years there is too little water in the canals of these four projects. The result is that in July, August and September, just when the water is most needed, there is a falling off and frequently there is an acute shortage of water, especially if the snowfall in the mountains has not been adequate during the previous winter, or if there has been hot weather melting the snow' rapidly in the early weeks of the year. We have known at least forty per cent too little water in the ditches right at a time when growing was most important.
In the St. Mary's river there is at the present time not a reservoir in which water can be stored and from which the water in the ditches can be supplemented. There is considerable water in Alberta if only we could store it and have it available. There is enough water in four rivers in my constituency to supply all the area in that constituency and some of the area in other constituencies, particularly Medicine Hat. There are four rivers, namely, Waterton, Belly, St. Mary's and Milk, all in southwestern Alberta. From these rivers there is available for use in irrigation 795,700 acre feet of water. This quantity, allowing for losses from evaporation and seepage, would supply the needs of 465,000 acres of land. There is a particular matter of urgency in connection with' this area. The St. Mary's and Milk rivers are both so nearly international streams that the United States has a claim to a share of the water. Back in 1901 the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company began to build a canal from which the 
Magrath, Raymond and Lethbridge areas are now watered. Then a reclamation act was passed by the congress of the United States in 1902. The St. Mary's and Milk rivers project in Montana was authorized in 1903, and there were protests from citizens on both sides of the line, those on one side fearing that the people on the other side would. get more than their share.
In consequence, a boundary waters treaty was made on January 11, 1909, in which, under article. VI, there was set up an international joint commission to deal with the boundary waters. This provided for an apportionment of waters between the two countries under the direction of the commission. In the final act of the international joint commission on October 4, 1921, definite rules were laid down for dividing the water between Canada and the United States. In accordance with the final act, Canada, between 1922 and 1940, would receive annually from the St. Mary's and Milk rivers 403,200 acre-feet of water, and the United States, 324,100 acre-feet.
During' the years from 1922 to 1940 and since, Canada has wasted and is now wasting 55 per cent, of her share of the St. Mary's and 95 per cent of her share of the Milk river. This is extremely serious for two reasons. First, there is loss of production and of human values, and, second, there is danger of our losing our right to this water. It is recognized that a country must make beneficial use of water if it is to retain its right thereto. Canada for twenty-five years has neglected to make such beneficial use of her share of this water.
Realization of this fact will make it clear to hon. members why the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is very wisely planning to begin active work on the construction of the St. Mary's river project this year. It is in order to protect our right to the water, and I wish to commend him very highly and to express to him once more the gratitude of my constituents for his promptness in going forward with this work immediately upon the cessation of the war.
Meanwhile, what has the United States been doing with her share? The United States authorized her St. Mary's and Milk river project in 1903 and began work in 1906, completing it in 1920. She has built the Sherbourne reservoir, capable of storing 66,000 acre-feet near the head1 of the St. Mary's, and a diversion canal from the St. Mary's to the Milk river to carry into the Milk the United1 States share of the St. Mary's. Then, near the Milk river she has constructed the Fresno reservoir,

Water Conservation
capable of storing 126,000 acre-feet and the Nelson river reservoir, capable of storing 66,800 acre-feet.
It is estimated that the United States is now equipped! to handle h$r share and ours as well, and all her share of the water is being beneficially used*. She has great need for much more than she has available, and she is finding irrigation profitable, as has been pointed out several times in the debate to-day. Thus again hon. members can see why the Minister of Agriculture has taken particular care to go ' forward with the construction of this project as expeditiously as possible.
The dam which we need to construct in Canada in order to show our good faith is what is known as the St. Mary's river dam. This dam is situated at Spring Coulee in my constituency. Its capacity will be 270,000 acre-feet. Into it can be diverted water from the Waterton river and the Belly river. Once this dam is constructed, once this reservoir is being used, there will be no occasion for anyone from the United States to establish the idea that Canada is not making beneficial use of her water. Thus the minister is proceeding with construction of the St. Mary's river dam. From the St. Mary's river dam, water can be carried to supply all the present projects to which I have referred' and to the seven other reservoirs in the district, and all these together will store enough water to supply the needs of all the present irrigation projects, and
345,000	acres of land which have not yet been brought under water.
Consequently this dam is of extremely great importance. The minister has told us to-day that $750,000 is to be spent on this dam this year. The total cost of the dam will be in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000. The reason why $750,000 is to be spent this year rather than the whole amount is that the dam cannot be built any faster. That is indicated by the apportionment of that sum of $750,000, which is about all that can be spent this year. In the second year the reservoir and outlet canals can be built at a cost of $2,250,000. Hon. members might therefore expect next year that the amount of money which will be set aside for the construction of the St. Mary's river dam will be $2,250,000. In the third year the reservoir, canal enlargement and distribution system would be built according to plan. This cost will be something over $2,250,000, estimated at pre-war prices.
There are four reasons, then, why we should go forward with this particular project as rapidly as we possibly can. The first one is the food situation; the second one is the possible war needs, for apparently we are not yet through with wars; the third one is the 63260-43J
rehabilitation of our boys, and finally, once more, the protection of our share of the water from the St Mary's and Milk rivers.
May I refer for just a moment to the general resolution? At the outset of my remarks I pointed out that the resolution does not really call .for the construction of the great irrigation system, although unquestionably it is the construction of the great irrigation system which is near to the heart of the hon. member for Davenport. I honour him greatly because of his deep interest and activity with respect to the popularization of the idea of constructing this great irrigation scheme. Since he spoke this afternoon, there has come into my hands the map of the whole area to which he referred. ' I wish to congratulate him again on that map. Many things are shown in detail. To my mind it is a splendid conception. I heartily support the idea. As a resident of Alberta, as a member for Alberta, let me say to the house that we in Alberta have no desire to have more of the water than is our share. We desire to see the other provinces have the advantage of water. We believe there is pleny of water in these rivers flowing down from the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains to supply the needs of all three provinces. The hon. member for Davenport expressed that idea this afternoon. From what studies I have been able to make I feel that I am justified in agreeing with him that there is plenty of water.
The next idea that was near to his heart,, and which he made quite clear to the house, was that of protecting the forests on the-slopes of the mountains. This must be done.. Once more I am heartily in accord with that idea. I believe, of course, that dominion money must go into the protection of those-forests, for the simple reason that one province simply cannot take care of the great problem which is involved in looking after those areas. All anyone needs to do is to look 'at a map, look at the Rocky mountains as they skirt the western boundary of Alberta, estimate the tremendous length of those mountains, estimate the amount of money which would have to be spent in order to have suitable precautions made ready to act in emergencies, such as fire hazards. Anyone can recognize that no one province in this dominion would be in a position to discharge the financial responsibilities involved. There simply must be assistance from the dominion government. This does not mean that Alberta should surrender any of her rights under the British North America Act, any of her resources or any of her property and civil rights. It does mean that assistance must
Water Conservation

come from the other provinces to protect the resource which is of vital interest to all the people of Canada.
I now find myself in a difficult position. I have to repeat once more that I favour com' pletely the establishment of an elaborate, far-reaching thorough-going irrigation system throughout the three prairie provinces, and I favour the protection of the forests on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. But I cannot say that I favour the idea of the dominion government passing a law to set up a commission to do what this resolution calls for. There is no objection to having a committee study the situation. I think there is no danger in the wording. In that respect may I read it again. This commission is to be set up to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river. So far as I can see, there can be no objection to that if this committee has no power or authority to rule with respect to the use of the water. However, I believe the minister's point was well taken when he indicated quite clearly that it is not the proper function of the dominion government to take the initiative in this matter, especially since the provinces themselves, through their representatives, have met and proceeded to do the work which is envisaged by this resolution.
THOMAS REID (New Westminster): I ur^^lre to say a few words on this resolution. First of all, may I commend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) for bringing the resolution before the house. He is one of those members who have, in the words of the man on the street, what is called a roving commission. He has taken it upon himself to interest himself in parts of Canada other than his own particular riding. Perhaps he may have a little more time and may be a little better fixed financially than many other hon. members to do this, and then he is not easily intimidated with respect to going into other members' ridings and investigating what is going on there.
On various occasions the hon. member has introduced most commendable resolutions. In commending him to-night I wish at the same time to say something on the principle of the resolution. It may seem strange that one from British Columbia should rise at this late stage of the debate and deal with a resolution which refers particularly to the watershed of the Saskatchewan river. It is no more strange than the hon. member for Davenport introducing it.

As I say, I intend to deal with the resolution itself. In that regard I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who in his opening remarks drew the attention of the house to the fact that this resolution might infringe upon provincial rights.	[DOT]
I know there are many members in the house who do not view the infringement of provincial rights by the dominion as seriously as I do. Ever since 1939 when the dominion took over all tjoe powers of the country many municipal and provincial governments have been set aside. As a matter of fact, in many instances provincial governments have been nothing more than glorified municipal councils, at least for the past six years. People have become so accustomed to the dominion government handling their affairs that their eyes turn to Ottawa. If their chickens do not lay, it must be the fault of the dominion government. If there is trouble at home, it must be the fault of the dominion government. On every occasion the provincial governments will be found looking to Ottawa for assistance and help. I view that tendency with alarm. I view as one who lives some three thousand miles from Ottawa viewing with alarm the centralization of power in Ottawa. I would advise members of parliament to give a little more thought to asking the dominion government to do everything within their province or within their municipality. Bit by bit power is being concentrated in the city of Ottawa, and I say the time is not yet ripe, in the interests of the welfare of the people, that all power should be centralized here.
I listened with a great deal of attention while the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) read the voluminous correspondence which has passed between the dominion government and certain provincial premiers, in which the discussion centred around the eastern watershed and the taking off. of trees from the mountain-tops. The removal of the trees from both heights of land and from the mountains as well has done irreparable damage to farm land not only close to the Rocky mountains but in the other western provinces as well. In the province from which I come there was a time when the forests in the Fraser valley held the water right through the growing season. In those years the farmers had not the difficulties they have experienced since. The rain that fell in the winter and spring was held in the soil for months, generally speaking, and percolated very slowly to the creeks and rivers. Once the timber was cut off, however, the rain which fell in the winter and spring ran right off, of course

Water Conservation
causing floods during the spring season. Something else was caused in the summer time, however; a dryness resulted which has affected the growing of crops for many long years.
I remember an incident which occurred in 1932 or 1933, when under the administration of that day men were put to work cutting trees off the mountains in a district called Lillooet. The only purpose in having those men cut the trees from the mountain-tops and mountain-side was to keep the snow from hanging, although those men might have been given other and more useful work, because Lillooet is a gold centre and men were and still are making anywhere from $2 to $16 a day panning gold. But taking off that timber did irreparable damage to the district of Lillooet, and the same thing occurred in the Fraser district.
I should like to have seen a resolution of this kind broadened, not to ask the dominion government to take over irrigation projects but merely to ask it to make a survey and advise the provinces as to what should be done in regard to irrigation. Something has been said about planned economy; I believe I heard one speaker mention that this evening. From my knowledge of the prairies I believe I am correct in saying that, at the most, irrigation would affect but a fraction of the prairie land. Out of some sixty or sixty-five million acres of land, of which some twenty or thirty millions are in the prairie belt, I doubt if more than two or three million acres at the most could be brought under irrigation. It is all very well to talk about producing more food, about planned economy, and so on, and to place before the people a picture in which the whole prairie district will be helped out by some great water scheme. But for the benefit of the farmers on the prairies and some hon. members who advocate this scheme, after some practical experience I am going to predict that when that type of farming comes to the prairies many who are looking forward to it may not care to farm under it.
With irrigation you have to farm with a shovel. The irrigation ditches are all put down; but once you start irrigation you cannot just sit on your fanny and pray that the Lord will bring some rain, or send for a Hatfield to bring rain. You cannot do that any more. Once you get into irrigation you have really to work; and after a man has sat on his fanny for ten or fifteen years on the prairies, once he has to get hold of a shovel and work all day going out through the rows of trees or out among his crops he may not like it. Yet if he does not do that the water system will not be worth anything at all;
I do not think any hon. member will dispute-that. I know a district in the middle of British Columbia where a certain type of farmer has taken up the growing of apples and other crops under irrigation. Those farmers have gone into that district because they are not afraid of work, and because they know what they have to put up with. But I am thinking of those who have long sat looking to the clouds or to the dominion government or to a Hatfield to bring them what they need, and I am just wondering how they will like it after these irrigation schemes are put into effect. I am not too sure that they will take kindly to it. I know that many who come from the prairies to British Columbia find farming there just a little tougher than they found it in Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba, although perhaps when we get into the new era that may be changed.
My main purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, was to draw the attention of hon. members to the principles at stake in this proposal, and to advise hon. members to view with care putting into the hands of the dominion government powers which properly should belong to the provincial governments.

which is variously estimated at 100, 200, 300 and even $400 million, that this house is perfectly entitled to discuss such an important question for at least a whole day.
I am not one of those who waste their time in discussions on what the east could do for the west and vice versa. I know too well the good understanding that exists among our people to waste time in such idle talk. A lot is said that is jocularly but I know that in Montreal, Toronto and even in the maritime provinces, our conditions are perfectly well known. I realize the vast sums of money that were expended to open the western prairies, where I live, but I also know that they have created considerable wealth in return, to an amount which certainly balances the expenditures involved.
I well remember, Mr. Speaker, that in normal times-and I hope they will return-I well remember that the topic of the day in the month of August boiled down, for western farmers as well as for the rest of the country, to wondering about the crop out west. Would the prairie provinces have a bumper crop? The Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg newspapers and those of other cities as well sent reporters and experts to gauge the crop prospects out west. Factories in our industrial centres anxiously awaited reports on the wheat crop of western farmers. Would we reap one hundred, two hundred or three hundred million bushels of wheat? That was the topic of the day, Mr. Speaker, because western farmers, who operate on a large scale, supply with funds the factories v as well as wholesale and retail dealers of the central and eastern provinces.
Sometimes I incline to think that the western farmer is to a certain extent a spendthrift. Then, let us stop discussing projects as extensive as the one which has been proposed by the hon. member for Davenport, who considers it rather as from a local issue, while I view it as having a national character. I was saying, in the course of the remarks I made in English, that about fifty-four years ago this month. I was travelling with my father and a neighbour who were chatting on the train that was moving slowly across the great western plains. Those plains looked extensive to us, outsiders, who were from the Lake St. John district, where, as you all know, the plains do not cover very great stretches- when I was a boy, I remember that our small pasture seemed very near the house. Needless to say how astonished I was when I saw those great plains which seemed to extend so far in the distance, that we could not think we would ever reach the end: It was then
[Mr. Dechene.1
that I asked my companion: "How is it that these lands are not afl under cultivation?" Why are those plains not already peopled all over? Why do the wheat fields not stretch as far as the eye can reach? That is what happens to-day in the irrigated areas or where the rainfall is plentiful. And my old companion answered right back: "Well, my friend, do you see any trees in these plains?" "As a matter of fact, I do not". "Well, that is because we have no rain. The lack of timber in these vast areas is due to the lack of rain."

Indeed, as the eastern slope of the Rockies is stripped of its vegetation, and as the snow-fields, which were so beneficial to us in past years, recede, water gets scarcer in the western prairies, the velocity of our rivers decreases, humidity gradually disappears everywhere. As a result, the dry regions of the western provinces increase in area, except, possibly, in ' Manitoba. This is a vital problem which will command our serious attention at some future time, but, of course, it cannot be considered with a province that will not cooperate. In my opinion, the hon. member for Davenport should have sought first of all, with his customary courtesy, an interview with the leaders of the Alberta government in order to ascertain whether the latter were prepared to cooperate with the dominion government in carrying out such a measure. But as the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) has shown by means of the correspondence exchange with the leaders of that province, they are not prepared to cooperate in carrying out the work essential to the project which was so ably introduced by the hon. member for Davenport.
As I stated a moment ago, rainfall is getting more and more scanty from year to year in the northern section of Alberta, of Saskatchewan right up to my own district in the vicinity of Cold lake. There lies the vital problem which prompts me to join with the hon. members who have spoken on this matter * in asking the whole house to consider very seriously this matter of irrigation in that part of the western provinces. We must act now, but not in the manner suggested in the resolution. In fact, I do not think it wise to insist on such a vote being taken, when the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who represents his party in the house to-night, is apparently unable to make up his mind. This matter should be submitted in such a way that the house could unanimously support a resolution which should be endorsed by hon. members in every section of the house.
As I said a moment ago in English, the province of Alberta is carrying on a rather costly experiment in the way of irrigation-[DOT]

the same meaning as the original. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for having called my attention to the rules of the house. If I broke those rules, I beg your forgiveness. The resolution is worded as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of introducing legislation during this session to set up a permanent interprovincial board or commission . . .
The province of Alberta is therefore included.
... on which the three prairie provinces and the dominion . . .
Again the province of Alberta is included.
. . . would have equal representation under the chairmanship of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or some other qualified person, to conduct investigations and make studies of the most feasible and economic means for the conservation and utilization of the eastern watershed of the Rocky mountains, particularly the watershed of the Saskatchewan river.
Mr. Speaker, I was just discussing that point. I was saying that some of this water flows in the plain, gradually reaches to the northlands and even further. This water, however, does not flow with the same abundance as in the southern areas of the prairies, but , . .
